title: Start solving: a practical introduction
summary: Find the right pages, reproduce known results, and turn an idea into a test someone else can repeat.
text:
Liber Primus combines visible artwork, rune text, numbers, and hidden file content. Learn how these layers differ before treating them as one cipher. A title image can have no runic paragraph and still carry a signed OutGuess message.

1. Know the collection
The first release contains 17 images, including two title pages. The second release contains 58. In the archived source snapshot, LP1 has known readings and LP2 has readings for 56 and 57; LP2 pages 00–55 remain unsolved. This is dated documented knowledge, not live proof that nobody has solved anything else.
Use IDs such as LP2-31. “Page 31” without a release or archive name is ambiguous. The numbering cross-reference maps release IDs to archive filenames.

The illustrated cover with compasses comes from an earlier puzzle stage and has its own entry. It is different from LP1-00, the plain title page, and does not change the release numbering.

[Image: The warning page used for the first reading exercise]
LP1-01: start here. Its known Atbash reading makes a short, checkable first exercise.
[Image: LP2-31, an unsolved page used in the statistics guide]
LP2-31: a later investigation. Its recorded measurements describe the text; they do not supply a decryption.

2. Reproduce one short reading
Open the warning in the reader. Compare the original image with its runes, then follow the complete warning reading and its Atbash explanation. Use the 29-symbol alphabet, not English A–Z. Count a multi-letter rune as one symbol.

python scripts/verify_bundle.py REFERENCE-DATA-CONTENTS.json
python scripts/reproduce_reading.py warning
python scripts/reproduce_reading.py --check-all
Download and extract the reference-data ZIP, then run these commands from the extracted folder with Python 3. Keep the folders together: the script reads the included text and parameter files. After the file check, the warning command prints its literal reading; --check-all checks all 17 known runic-page outputs. All three commands run locally with the Python standard library and make no AI requests. A full repository checkout also works.

The first command checks the extracted files against the bundle’s own manifest and should report 0 problems. It does not authenticate the manifest. If it reports missing or changed files, follow the setup check before interpreting a decoding result.

What success looks like

The warning output begins A-WARNNG.BELIEUE-NOTHNG-FROM-. Those spellings are expected literal rune labels, not evidence that the script failed. The complete control check prints:

PASS: 17 literal page readings match the published controls exactly.

This confirms that the supplied recipes reproduce the stored known outputs. It does not independently authenticate the source files or validate a proposed solution to an unsolved page. Use the download catalogue for file hashes and the transliteration guide for the difference between literal labels and contextual English.

Working from a phone? You can do the first arithmetic check without installing anything. In the worked warning example, the first rune has index 4. Subtracting it from 28 gives 24, the label A. The next input index is 21, giving 7, or W. Follow the table against the original image, then read the complete passage. Save the script run for when you have a Python environment.

Optional second check: one row of the number grid
Open LP1-05 and find the five-by-five grid below the text. Its first row mixes four printed numbers with one rune word. In the known reading that word is labeled SHADOWS.
Leave the printed entries 272, 138, 131 and 151 unchanged.
Use the worked rune-cell table to check the word’s seven rune values. Their sum is 341.
Add the row: 272 + 138 + 341 + 131 + 151 = 1033.
This verifies one row, not the whole square. The full explanation shows all five rows, five columns and two main diagonals. If you have Python, python scripts/check_number_examples.py reproduces those checks from the included page and alphabet records.
The important distinction is the input: the printed decimal numbers stay as numbers, while rune words are replaced by additive prime values. Do not apply a prime-index lookup to every entry or replace the words with ordinary English spelling. Those would be different procedures.
New to the terminal? Running the reproduction scripts walks through setup, expected results, trace columns, and common errors.
3. Learn the other layers
Rune indices and prime values: cipher arithmetic versus prime sums.
Vigenère: keys, direction, and continuity across pages.
The cover payload chain: OutGuess, hexadecimal, XOR, signatures, and transposition.
Spelling and prime sums: a reproducible numerical property versus an explanation of a spelling’s purpose.

For the ideas behind the decoded passages, follow the philosophy reading route, then compare the William Blake parallel. These guides distinguish the manuscript words, interpretation, and possible outside sources.

4. Make an idea testable
Choose a page, a region, a transformation, and a success criterion. “Try primes” is too broad. “Subtract consecutive prime-minus-one values modulo 29 from LP2-31, starting at the first rune, advancing the prime sequence only for runes, continuing across punctuation without resetting, and skipping no runes” specifies one test. It does not establish that this is the correct method.
Check Have we tried it? for the technique and scope. The registry is awaiting reviewed records; an empty result means no published match here, not that an idea is new. Follow the reproducibility guide.

Choose one first investigation

You do not need to learn every technique at once. Choose a route that produces a small result someone else can inspect.

	If you want to…	Start with	Keep as your result

	Read and interpret	Compare the warning and later instructions	Exact passages, their locations, and your interpretation stated separately

	Inspect artwork	Compare the insect drawings	Page IDs, visible similarities and differences, and any named comparison source

	Check arithmetic	Reproduce LP1-05’s mixed-grid conversion	The original cells, rune-value substitutions, and all twelve line sums

	Measure a text	Reproduce LP2-31’s IoC	The input hash, rune counts, exact fraction, and a statement of what it cannot establish

	Study a decoding	Trace the Welcome’s repeating key	A few input/output steps, the key position, and the treatment of recorded exceptions


Before expanding a numerical search, check what your operation preserves. For example, whole-stream IoC cannot choose between rearrangements of the same symbols. For literary or visual work, a well-supported comparison is useful even when it supplies no cipher key.

A first observation using only your phone

Open LP2-49 in the reader. Beneath the three runic rows, find the third row of the letter-and-number grid. Count grid rows from one and columns from left to right. This row reads:

21 3M 0F 0X 1g 2H 0x 1R

[Image: Third grid row of LP2-49, including uppercase 0X in column four and lowercase 0x in column seven.]
Detail from the original JPEG, region [600, 1560, 1200, 160]. Download the complete original.

Compare column 4, 0X, with column 7, 0x. The initial character is zero in the archived transcription; the second character differs in case.
Write the observation with its location: “LP2-49, grid row 3: column 4 is transcribed as 0X; column 7 as 0x.”
Keep a proposed explanation separate. This difference does not yet tell you whether the entries encode letters, coordinates, or numbers.

You have now made a small claim another reader can check. The grid transcription guide explains ambiguous characters and leading zeroes; its coordinate exports let you check the same positions in structured data. If you disagree with a glyph, preserve the original transcription and document the proposed correction with the image location.

Find the page behind a quotation

Suppose you remember the phrase “circumference practices” and want to cite it. A complete reading can cover several sheets, so finding the section is only the first step.


Search for "circumference practices", including the quotation marks. LP1-10 is the literal-reading match. Other sheets can appear because their records include the same complete section text.

Open LP1-10’s known reading. The word crosses its first two literal lines: CIRCU/ then MFERENCE. Compare the page’s original image when checking the underlying runes.

Keep the location with your note: “LP1-10, literal reading, lines 1–2; word joined across the line break.” A statement about what the circumference means is your interpretation and needs its own explanation.


With Python, repeat the lookup using python scripts/reading_concordance.py "circumference practices" --literal. Add --json to retain the exact excerpt, character offsets, and page-record checksum. The concordance guide explains those fields and why character positions are not rune indices. This exercise works with a known reading; it does not search for English words inside unsolved ciphertext.

Ready to contribute
You should be able to identify an exact image, distinguish raw from corrected transcription, reproduce a known reading, and explain what would count against your hypothesis. You do not need to understand every cipher before inspecting a well-defined detail.
For a worked descriptive analysis, use the index-of-coincidence baseline: exact rune counts, downloadable results, reproduction commands and the limits of frequency evidence.
Sources and verification
Pinned historical walkthrough. Recipes reproduce published controls; they are not new solutions. Local computational verification: 19 October 2026.

title: Running the reproduction scripts
summary: Set up the repository, verify a known reading, understand a rune-by-rune trace, and diagnose common errors.
text:
Reproducing a reading means starting with the manuscript's rune text, applying the documented cipher, and checking that you get the same result. It is a useful first step into solving: you can see how a method works before changing it or trying it on an unsolved page.

This walkthrough uses LP1-01, the warning. Its Atbash cipher reverses the rune alphabet, so you can follow the calculation by hand as well as run it in Python. By the end, you will have decoded the page, checked your result, and inspected the first two runes step by step.

1. Download and open the files

Download the reference-data ZIP and extract it into an empty folder. Open that folder: you should see directories named scripts, text and data. Keep them together. The script supplies the instructions; the other folders supply the manuscript text, cipher settings and known readings it needs.

Open START-HERE.txt in the extracted folder for a task-by-task command list: decode a known reading, find a phrase, measure rune distributions, locate repeats, or replay an earlier puzzle chain. You can also read those instructions before downloading.

Open a terminal in this folder. A terminal is the window where you type the commands below. On Windows, you can use File Explorer's Open in Terminal command. If you navigate there with cd, put quotation marks around a folder path that contains spaces.

The reference-data ZIP is enough for this walkthrough. If you want to edit the site or work with draft experiments, get the complete repository instead using Code → Download ZIP. Readers who already use Git can clone it:

git clone https://github.com/jelliottdev/jelliottdev.github.io.git
cd jelliottdev.github.io

2. Check Python

You need Python 3. On Windows, try py --version; on macOS or Linux, try python3 --version. If neither command is available, install Python from the official Python downloads or your operating system’s package manager, then reopen your terminal. A command that prints a Python 2 version is not suitable.

	Terminal	Run the warning example
	Windows PowerShell	py scripts/reproduce_reading.py warning
	macOS / Linux	python3 scripts/reproduce_reading.py warning
	If python already selects Python 3	python scripts/reproduce_reading.py warning

The wiki’s other recipes use python as shorthand. Substitute the command that worked on your machine; the script path and arguments stay the same. The calculation runs on your computer; it does not use the site's AI assistant.

3. Decode the warning and check the result

Check the extracted files first

Before decoding, check that the extracted files match the bundle’s recorded sizes and hashes. Run this from the folder containing scripts, text and data, using the Python command that worked above:

python scripts/verify_bundle.py REFERENCE-DATA-CONTENTS.json

A successful check reports a file count followed by 0 problems. The count can change as the wiki grows. Missing or changed files are listed with FAIL:, and the command exits unsuccessfully. The checker reads files without modifying them; files you add yourself are outside its manifest and are not checked.

This is a check against the included manifest, not independent proof of who created it. You can also compare the ZIP itself with the download catalogue. See bundle verification for the distinction between checking the archive and checking its contents.

Run the known control

Run the warning command from the table above. In the examples that follow, python means whichever Python 3 command worked on your machine.

python scripts/reproduce_reading.py warning

The script reads LP1-01, applies Atbash, and compares its output with the stored reading. It then prints === LP1-01 === followed by the decoded text. Open the complete warning reading beside it to compare the output with the explanation.

The spelling may look unusual. The output uses literal rune labels, which preserve distinctions that ordinary English can hide. Keep those spellings when checking the result; the guide also provides contextual English to help you read the message.

Once this example works, check the other known readings:

python scripts/reproduce_reading.py --list
python scripts/reproduce_reading.py --check-all

--list shows the nine named sections available to the script. --check-all decodes them and should finish with:

PASS: 17 literal page readings match the published controls exactly.

A control is an example whose expected result is already known. Matching it helps check that the implementation and inputs work together. There are nine sections but 17 pages because some sections span several images. This command checks those known readings; it does not attempt the unsolved pages or extract hidden image content.

4. Read a rune-by-rune trace

python scripts/reproduce_reading.py warning --trace

A trace shows the intermediate steps rather than only the finished text. Here, each row follows one rune from its input alphabet position to its output. The format is CSV (comma-separated values), so you can also open it in a spreadsheet. The first two rows are:

page,page_rune_ordinal,section_rune_ordinal,input_rune,input_index,subtracted_value,output_index,latin,copied
lp1-01,0,0,ᚱ,4,,24,A,False
lp1-01,1,1,ᛝ,21,,7,W,False

Atbash maps index x to 28 − x. The first rune has index 4, so its output index is 24, labeled A. The second has index 21, so its output is 7, labeled W. These are zero-based alphabet indices, not prime values. A two-letter Latin label such as NG still represents one rune.

You only need the input index, output index and Latin label to follow this Atbash example. The remaining fields help when a method crosses page boundaries or skips particular runes:

	Field	Meaning

	page_rune_ordinal	Zero-based rune position within the page; resets at each new page.

	section_rune_ordinal	Position under the control’s section/boundary rule. It can continue across pages.

	input_index, output_index	Positions in the 29-rune alphabet before and after the transformation.

	subtracted_value	The applied Vigenère or prime-minus-one amount. Blank for Atbash, direct reading, or a copied interruption; blank is not a recorded zero.

	latin	The output rune’s Latin label, before contextual English editing.

	copied	Whether this position is listed as an interruption in the control. False does not mean the index changed: direct readings also have false entries.


Non-rune characters are preserved in the literal output but do not get trace rows. For a key-dependent example, run python scripts/reproduce_reading.py welcome --trace and follow keystream positions and interruptions. The specific LP1-10 correction is applied before transformation and trace output; see transcription layers.

Save a reading or trace

Use --output to keep the result as a file. The script checks the reading against its stored control before writing anything, saves UTF-8 text, and refuses to replace an existing file.

python scripts/reproduce_reading.py warning --output warning.txt
python scripts/reproduce_reading.py warning --trace --output warning-trace.csv

The filenames above are created in your terminal’s current folder. You can choose another existing folder; quote the path if it contains spaces. The script does not create missing folders. The text file contains the same page headings and literal reading as the terminal output. The CSV contains only the header and trace rows; the “Saved” confirmation is printed to the terminal, not inserted into the file.

When importing the CSV into a spreadsheet, select UTF-8 and a comma delimiter if asked. Each rune has its own row. A multi-page section such as Welcome keeps the page ID in every row, so the trace can be filtered without losing its page attribution. Keep this original export alongside any spreadsheet you edit.

This option saves a named section, with or without --trace; it does not combine with --list or --check-all. A saved trace documents the known control’s computation, not a new experiment on an unsolved page.

When you are ready to try another method

The warning example needs only Python and the reference-data bundle. Other tasks work on different layers of the manuscript. Reconstructing already-extracted text is different from extracting it from a JPEG yourself, which is why their software requirements differ.

For image-based work, extract the original-images ZIP into the same folder as the reference data. See the bundle instructions for the complete command list.

Check those image files with python scripts/verify_bundle.py ORIGINAL-IMAGES-CONTENTS.json. Each download has a separately named manifest. Prefer these names to the generic CONTENTS.json, which another bundle may replace when extracted into the same folder. Passing the reference-data check does not check images from the image bundle.

	Task	Requirements	Instructions

	Known rune readings	Python 3, standard library only	Warning control

	Locate words in known readings	Python 3, standard library only; searches contextual English	Known-reading concordance

	Reproduce rune prime sums	Python 3, standard library only; uses decoded rune sequences	Prime-sum checks

	Check prime positions and numerical examples	Python 3, standard library only	Prime values and positions

	Recompute whole-page IoC	Python 3, standard library only; uses archived rune streams	IoC baseline

	Measure single-rune entropy	Python 3, standard library only; uses the archived frequency counts	Entropy examples and limits

	Locate repeated rune sequences	Python 3, standard library only; reports overlapping windows and source positions	Bigram and trigram reports

	Redraw the frequency chart	Python 3 and Matplotlib; reads the saved IoC counts	Frequency chart and command

	Reconstruct the exported cover chain	Python 3, standard library only; uses stored extractions	Cover chain

	Reproduce the illustrated-cover RSA message	Python 3, standard library only; uses the recorded factors and stored payload	RSA reproduction

	Reproduce the Emerson book cipher	Python 3, standard library only for the stored paragraph source	Book-cipher reproduction

	Check visual-record structure	Python 3, standard library only	Opening-page inventory

	Recount image pixels with --pixels	Python 3 and Pillow	Image regions and measurement rules

	Extract hidden JPEG payloads again	Python wrapper plus an OutGuess executable	OutGuess extraction

	Verify signed messages	GnuPG and the documented public key	PGP signatures


Install an optional package only when you need it

You can complete the warning walkthrough, prime-sum checks, concordance, and IoC calculation without installing any Python packages. To redraw the chart, install Matplotlib into the same Python environment that will run the plotting script. To recount image pixels, install Pillow. The package names and Python import names differ for Pillow: its code is imported as PIL.

python -m pip install matplotlib
python scripts/plot_rune_frequencies.py --output my-rune-frequencies.svg

The installation command may download packages; the plotting command reads local files. If you use py or python3 for the scripts, use that same command before -m pip. This avoids installing a package for one Python interpreter and running the script with another.

For a separate project environment, create a local .venv folder and invoke its Python directly. Activation is optional:

Windows PowerShell

py -m venv .venv
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install matplotlib
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe scripts/plot_rune_frequencies.py --output my-rune-frequencies.svg

macOS / Linux

python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/python -m pip install matplotlib
.venv/bin/python scripts/plot_rune_frequencies.py --output my-rune-frequencies.svg

Keep the environment separate from the preserved evidence files. Record package versions when sharing a generated figure: python -m pip show matplotlib reports the installed version. Visual output can vary across package or font versions even when the underlying numerical counts agree.

When a command fails

“Command not found” or “not recognized”: check the Python command first. If it names outguess or gpg, that is a separate executable, not a missing rune dataset.

“Can’t open file” for the script: check the terminal’s current folder. Open the extracted folder that contains scripts, rather than its parent folder or the ZIP itself.

A missing text/ or data/ file: extract a fresh reference-data bundle and keep its directories together. Moving just the script breaks the relative paths it uses to find its inputs.

No module named matplotlib or No module named PIL: install the optional package for the Python interpreter running that particular task. Neither error means the basic reading checks need those packages.

“Output already exists”: choose a new output filename or inspect the existing result. Scripts that refuse overwrites do so to preserve earlier output, not because the calculation failed.

Boxes instead of runes: the terminal font may lack runic characters. Check the numeric indices and Latin labels, and compare with the browser reader. Missing glyphs alone do not establish bad input bytes.

“Output differs” or a hash mismatch: preserve the full error and identify the affected file. Compare with an unchanged copy and the checksums. Do not change the expected output merely to make the check pass.

Keep the result reproducible

Record the repository commit, Python version, command, and output. In a Git checkout, git rev-parse HEAD prints the commit ID. For a ZIP download, retain the archive and its checksum; do not claim a commit ID you have not verified. When you move from a control to a new hypothesis, follow documenting a reproducible attempt. A passing control is a starting point, not evidence that the same method solves another page.

Reproducing rune prime sums provides a read-only command and explicit spelling comparisons.
Implementation and verification

The commands and trace fields above are documented from the reproduction script and its control parameters. The first trace rows and all 17 literal page outputs were checked locally on 19 October 2026. Operating-system launch commands are alternatives; this verification used Python 3.12 on Windows.

title: Transliteration and literal readings
summary: Keep manuscript symbols separate from the decisions made while interpreting them.
text:
Different text layers
A transcription records runes. A transliteration replaces each rune with a Latin label. A cipher transformation may produce plaintext rune indices, whose labels form a literal decoded reading. Contextual English can normalize spelling or interpret those labels. It is an editorial layer.
Transliterating encrypted runes does not decrypt them. Conversely, direct-reading sections need no nontrivial substitution.

Compare the right outputs
Begin with the image and archived rune text. Record corrections before applying a cipher. Compare a literal output with the page-level control, not a normalized paragraph spanning several pages. Preserve spelling when testing prime sums.
On LP1-10, a documented I/E order correction matters. The script swaps runes at zero-based ordinals 116 and 117; it does not rewrite every similar sequence. See the transcription guide.
The worked trace guide follows the first two warning runes from input indices to literal labels.
One row, several different counts

The first row of LP2-31 shows why a character count is not automatically a rune count. This page has no known reading in the source snapshot; the Latin labels below remain ciphertext labels.

[Image: First row of LP2-31, with black runes, small separators and a compact punctuation cluster.]
Original-image rectangle [570, 640, 1260, 180]. Open the complete page.

Compare the representations

Archived rune row:
ᚦᚳᛒᛝᛏᛉᛡᛞ-ᛋᛡ-ᚩᚠ.ᛈᛖᛞᛋᛁ-ᛚᛁᚻᚾᛝᚱ-/

Latin labels, with archive delimiters retained:
THCBNGTXIAD-SIA-OF.PEDSI-LIHNNGR-/

The archive row has 29 Unicode characters: 23 rune symbols, four hyphens, one period and one slash. This count excludes the newline that separates rows in the text file. The final slash records a line boundary; it is not an additional rune drawn at the right edge of the image. The other delimiter names follow the archive’s transcription convention.

The first four runes have labels TH · C · B · NG. Those are four symbols but six Latin letters. Concatenating the labels as THCBNG loses their individual boundaries unless the mapping is kept alongside them. Indexing that string one English letter at a time would therefore change the unit being analyzed. See rune indices and prime values.

Reproduce the counts

From an extracted reference-data bundle or repository checkout, save this as a Python file in the root directory and run it there. It uses only Python’s standard library and reads the preserved transcription:

import json
from collections import Counter
from pathlib import Path

index = json.loads(Path("data/index.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
labels = {item["rune"]: item["latin"] for item in index["alphabet"]}
row = Path("text/lp2-31.txt").read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines()[0]
runes = [char for char in row if char in labels]
other = Counter(char for char in row if char not in labels)
print("Archived characters:", len(row))
print("Runes:", len(runes))
print("Other characters:", dict(other))
print("First four labels:", [labels[char] for char in runes[:4]])

Expected output:
Archived characters: 29
Runes: 23
Other characters: {'-': 4, '.': 1, '/': 1}
First four labels: ['TH', 'C', 'B', 'NG']

Selecting only runes is appropriate for the published rune-frequency calculation. It is not a faithful copy of every visible feature. Keep the original row when testing punctuation, spacing or boundaries, and state whether a key advances on runes only or on another declared unit. A transcriber’s separator does not decide that rule for you. See printed marks and exported characters.

Sources and verification
Pinned historical walkthrough. Recipes reproduce published controls; they are not new solutions. Local computational verification: 19 October 2026.

title: Documenting a reproducible attempt
summary: Make the question, inputs, transformations, and limits checkable.
text:
Define the claim
Name page IDs, regions, input hashes, transcription versions, transformation order, key space, offsets, and boundary rules. State which parameters were fixed in advance and which were selected after viewing outputs.

Turn “try shifts” into a bounded question

The following is a candidate-generation example, not a completed hypothesis test. It shows how to specify a small search on LP2-31 without implying that the page is expected to use this method.

	Decision	Example specification

	Input	The archived text/lp2-31.txt, with its SHA-256 recorded at run time

	Symbols	Only the 29 recognized runes, including rune headings; punctuation and decimal digits excluded

	Order	The complete rune stream in its original order, or the complete stream reversed

	Transformation	For each order, subtract one fixed shift k modulo 29 from every rune index

	Bounds	Every integer k from 0 through 28; no skipped runes, alternate spellings, or extra transformations

	Outputs	All 58 labeled parameter cases, not only the most readable fragment

	Criterion	Before running, specify an independently motivated exact rune-index prefix or a fully defined scoring rule


There are 2 × 29 = 58 parameter cases. This is not a claim that all 58 output strings must be distinct. If you later try both including and excluding a heading, you have added another input choice. Record the new scope and count; do not describe the enlarged search as the original test.

“Looks like English” is not a sufficiently reproducible criterion on its own. An exact comparison needs the expected symbols and positions. A language score needs its formula, reference data, normalization, and selection rule. Whole-stream IoC is unsuitable for ranking this example’s cases because a fixed shift and a reversal preserve it; see what cipher operations preserve.

Generate the 58 cases yourself

Download and extract the reference-data bundle, then open a terminal in its extracted folder. With Python 3 installed, run:

python scripts/enumerate_shifts.py lp2-31 --output my-shifts.json

The script uses only Python’s standard library. It reads the archived transcription and writes all 58 cases to a new JSON file. It refuses to replace an existing file. No network connection or AI service is involved. For help with opening a terminal and checking downloaded files, see running the reproduction scripts.

Each case records its order, shift, and complete output as rune indices. For example, the invented input [0, 1, 28] with shift 1 becomes [28, 0, 27]. Reversing that input first gives [28, 1, 0], then subtracting 1 gives [27, 0, 28]. These small examples make the direction and order of operations visible.

	Report field	What it lets you check

	source_sha256	The exact archived input bytes used by this run.

	alphabet_runes_in_index_order	Which rune each index 0–28 denotes.

	rune_count	The length of the selected stream; LP2-31 currently contains 269 archived runes.

	case_count and distinct_output_count	How many parameter cases were generated, and how many different output sequences they produced. Those counts need not be equal.

	cases	Every original-order case followed by every reversed-order case, with shifts 0–28 in each group.


This command does not decide whether any candidate is meaningful. There is no language score, expected prefix, or success threshold in the script. Choose and document a comparison before examining the candidates if you intend to make a confirmatory claim. Generating this file does not publish an experiment or tell the idea checker that the technique has been ruled out.

Use known controls
A control has an expected result. Reproducing the warning checks an Atbash implementation; reproducing LP2-56 checks a particular prime schedule. One control does not validate every method or transcription.

Check the parts used by your own test. For the shift example, a short sequence with a hand-calculated result can detect an addition/subtraction error. A round trip checks that the inverse restores the input; an unchanged rune count checks that nothing was silently dropped. These checks serve different purposes. A round trip alone can pass even when encryption and decryption share the same mistaken convention.

For setup and a worked trace before writing your own attempt, see running the reproduction scripts.
What to record
The question and bounded tested scope.
Input paths, hashes, and explicit corrections.
A readable script, requirements, and copyable command.
Parameter bounds, random seeds, and candidate counts.
Expected and actual outputs, with the matching criterion.
What was not tested and what would change the conclusion.

Selection changes the evidence
Trying many spellings, boundaries, reversals and offsets creates opportunities for chance patterns. A probability claim must account for the selection process. A null model is the comparison process expected without the proposed mechanism; preserve relevant properties such as symbol counts or region lengths. There is no universal coincidence probability for an unspecified search.
Report “no match under these parameters,” not “the technique cannot work.” Label patterns selected after inspection as candidates for independent testing. See spelling and sums.

Worked distinctions: emirps and prime-index calculations.
For a complete numerical walkthrough, see null models and selection: six arrangements show exactly how choosing a pattern changes its chance comparison.

Write a conclusion that matches the run

Use these as wording patterns, not as results already obtained:

No exact match: “None of the 58 declared cases matched the specified prefix at the declared position.” This does not rule out different keys, transcriptions, regions, or a different expected prefix.
A high-scoring candidate: “This case ranked first under the stated score.” First place alone does not show that its score is unusual, that its text is meaningful, or that the method is correct.
Incomplete run: “The run stopped after these cases; the remaining cases were not checked.” An interrupted search is not a negative result for the full parameter range.

If a candidate prompted you to change a boundary or add an exception, keep the earlier outputs and label the revised test separately. The history explains which observations motivated which decisions. A new test can be useful without pretending its choices were made independently of the first result.

Make it easy for someone else to retest

Provide one command, the exact inputs, dependency versions, expected output location, and the comparison to perform. Keep the script readable and make failure visible: a missing file, unknown rune, or incomplete output should not quietly become an empty result. Store machine-readable results alongside an explanation of their fields.

A retest should compare the stated outputs, not merely confirm that the script exits successfully. Record who reviewed the result and what they checked. The registry’s published status requires that review; an example in this guide or a draft in the repository is not a published experiment record.

Create a draft in the repository
From a local checkout of the repository, run the scaffold command with a new, descriptive ID:
python scripts/new_experiment.py my-test-id
Replace my-test-id with lowercase words separated by hyphens. The command creates a folder under experiments/records/ with three files:
article.md: the question, rationale, pre-run plan, method, results, later changes, and retest explanation.
record.json: structured scope, inputs, outputs, hashes, and review fields used by the registry.
run.py: a stub that deliberately stops until you implement the test.
Complete the plan first. After the run, distinguish what completed from what was skipped or interrupted. Record any new exceptions or parameter choices prompted by the output, so another reader can see how the test developed. Leave the retest fields unfinished until someone has actually performed that check.
The scaffold starts as a draft and refuses to reuse an existing ID. Creating the files does not publish a result or add it to the idea checker. Follow the repository contribution instructions for validation and human review. The downloadable reference-data bundle is sufficient for the published examples; this contribution workflow uses the full repository checkout.
The research registry
Have we tried it? compares techniques and scope in published records. Background pages do not count as experiments. The registry remains empty while records are prepared and retested. The contribution format describes publication requirements.
For a worked descriptive analysis, use the index-of-coincidence baseline: exact rune counts, downloadable results, reproduction commands and the limits of frequency evidence.
Sources and verification
Pinned historical walkthrough. Recipes reproduce published controls; they are not new solutions. The linked known-reading recipes provide controls. The 58-case example demonstrates candidate generation. It does not test a plaintext hypothesis or report a decipherment.

title: Rune indices and prime values
summary: The same rune has an alphabet position and a separate Gematria Primus prime value.
text:
Two mappings, two jobs
The alphabet has 29 symbols. Its zero-based indices run from 0 to 28. Its prime values are the first 29 primes, from 2 to 109. F has index 0 and prime value 2; U has index 1 and prime value 3; TH has index 2 and prime value 5.
Known substitution ciphers use indices modulo 29. A Gematria Primus sum adds the prime values. Replacing one operation with the other changes the hypothesis.

See prime values and prime indices for the indexing convention and larger-number examples.
Index, ordinal position, and prime value

The first rune has index zero, but it uses the first prime. If p_(n) denotes the nth prime, the rune at alphabet index i has value p_(i + 1). The extra one converts zero-based alphabet indexing into one-based prime numbering.

	Rune / label	Alphabet index	Prime ordinal	Prime value

	ᚠ · F	0	1st	2

	ᚢ · U	1	2nd	3

	ᚦ · TH	2	3rd	5

	ᛠ · EA	28	29th	109


For example, subtracting the key index 1 from the rune TH gives (2 − 1) mod 29 = 1, which is U. Subtracting one from TH’s prime value instead gives 4, which is neither its new alphabet index under that rule nor a rune’s prime value. The operation must say which column it uses.

Count symbols, not Latin characters
TH, EO, NG and other multi-letter labels each denote a single rune. U/V and C/K renderings also require the stated convention. Work from runes when computing sums and offsets.

Reproduce a small example
For F–U–TH, the indices are [0, 1, 2] and the prime sum is 2 + 3 + 5 = 10. Atbash transforms the indices to [28, 27, 26]; it does not reverse the digits of the sum.
Next: modular arithmetic, literal readings, and worked spelling sums.
Reproducing rune prime sums provides a read-only command and explicit spelling comparisons.
Read the mappings from the reference data

From the extracted reference-data bundle or repository, save this as a Python 3 file and run it. It uses the alphabet stored in data/index.json, rather than a separately typed list of prime values.

import json
from pathlib import Path

alphabet = json.loads(Path("data/index.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))["alphabet"]
by_rune = {entry["rune"]: entry for entry in alphabet}
by_index = {entry["index"]: entry for entry in alphabet}
source = "ᚠᚢᚦ"
entries = [by_rune[rune] for rune in source]
indices = [entry["index"] for entry in entries]
prime_values = [entry["prime"] for entry in entries]
output = [by_index[28 - index]["latin"] for index in indices]

print("Indices:", indices)
print("Prime values:", prime_values)
print("Prime sum:", sum(prime_values))
print("Atbash labels:", "-".join(output))

Expected output:

Indices: [0, 1, 2]
Prime values: [2, 3, 5]
Prime sum: 10
Atbash labels: EA-IA-Y

The same three input runes support two separate calculations. The sum combines their prime values into one number; Atbash transforms each alphabet index and keeps three output symbols. Adding the input indices would give 3, a third calculation that should not be reported as the Gematria Primus sum.

This example accepts only the three runes shown. It deliberately does not strip punctuation or guess Latin spellings. When extending it to a manuscript passage, declare the text layer and separator rules first; use the prime-sum reproduction guide for complete known-reading examples.

Sources and verification

title: Arithmetic modulo 29
summary: How shifts wrap around the rune alphabet, including negative results.
text:
The rune alphabet has 29 positions, numbered 0 through 28. Arithmetic modulo 29 keeps a calculation within those positions by wrapping around whenever it passes either end. It supplies the arithmetic used by several documented readings, including Vigenère and prime-minus-one.

What “mod 29” means
Two integers are equal modulo 29 when their difference is a multiple of 29. For rune indices, choose the representative from 0 through 28. Moving forward from 28 by one returns to 0; moving backward from 0 by one returns to 28.

Worked steps
If ciphertext index c is 3 and the key value is 10, then p = (3 − 10) mod 29 = 22. First subtract normally to get −7. Then add 29 to choose the equivalent value in the allowed range. The negative intermediate result is not an error.

	Calculation	Ordinary result	Adjustment	Rune index

	28 + 1	29	Subtract 29	0

	0 − 1	−1	Add 29	28

	3 − 10	−7	Add 29	22

	21 − 256	−235	Add 9 × 29	26


The final row is a calculation from the LP2-56 trace. Eight additions of 29 leave −3; the ninth reaches 26. Adding 29 only once would also leave a negative number. A modulo operation handles however many complete turns are needed.

Different numbers can describe the same shift

A shift by 31 is equivalent to a shift by 2 because 31 = 29 + 2. Subtracting 23 is equivalent to adding 6 because −23 + 29 = 6. This explains how two walkthroughs can describe the same operation using different signed amounts.

Equivalence depends on the entire formula. Adding 23 and subtracting 23 are generally different. For input index 0, they produce 23 and 6 respectively. Do not change the direction while keeping the same key values and expect the same reading.

Modulo 29 is also different from writing a number in base 29. Modulo retains one residue; a base-29 representation expresses the whole number using place values. Likewise, reducing a Gematria Primus prime value modulo 29 does not generally recover the rune’s alphabet index. The value and index are separate assignments.

Python and JavaScript examples

For integer inputs and a positive divisor of 29, Python’s % gives the representative from 0 through 28:

def mod29(n):
    return n % 29

assert mod29(-7) == 22
assert mod29(-235) == 26
assert mod29(29) == 0
assert mod29(31) == 2
assert all(mod29(n) == mod29(n + 29) for n in range(-100, 101))

JavaScript’s % is a signed remainder operation: -7 % 29 gives −7. Normalize the result before using it as an alphabet index. The JavaScript remainder reference documents this distinction.

const mod29 = n => ((n % 29) + 29) % 29;

for (const [input, expected] of [[-7, 22], [-235, 26], [29, 0], [31, 2]]) {
    if (mod29(input) !== expected) throw new Error("Incorrect residue");
}

These examples are self-contained checks for small integers, not whole-page decoders. For an actual control, run python scripts/reproduce_reading.py lp2-56 --trace from the reference-data setup and inspect the input, subtracted value, and output columns.

Check a shift by undoing it

If decoding subtracts k, adding k back should recover the input modulo 29. For the example above, (22 + 10) mod 29 = 3. A round-trip check is useful for catching a sign or normalization mistake:

for c in range(29):
    for k in range(29):
        p = (c - k) % 29
        assert (p + k) % 29 == c

This verifies the arithmetic for every single-rune input and shift. It does not verify a keyword, a page transcription, or the handling of an interruption. Those choices belong to the complete decoding method.

What this does not decide
Modulo arithmetic supplies wraparound, not the key, direction, offset, or interruptions. See Vigenère, prime-minus-one, and keystream positions.
Sources and verification
Pinned historical walkthrough. Recipes reproduce published controls; they are not new solutions. The Python and JavaScript examples and all 841 single-rune shift round trips were checked on 20 October 2026.

title: Atbash and shifted Atbash
summary: Reverse the rune alphabet, with an extra shift where the control specifies one.
text:
The mapping
Ordinary Atbash gives p = 28 − c. Index 0 maps to 28, 1 to 27, and 14 to itself. Applying it twice returns the original index. It reverses the alphabet mapping, not rune order within a line.
The warning uses ordinary Atbash. The first koan, LP1-06–09, uses p = (28 − c + 3) mod 29. For c = 0 this produces index 2, because 31 mod 29 = 2.

Ordinary Atbash: pairs at opposite ends of the alphabet
ᚠ F · 0↔ᛠ EA · 28ᚢ U · 1↔ᛡ IA · 27ᛉ X · 14↔ᛉ X · 14
Each pair’s indices add to 28. The middle rune maps to itself. These examples show symbol substitutions, not a reversal of the order of text.

Follow the first runes

Use the zero-based rune indices, not the Gematria Primus prime values. Each input rune is replaced in its existing position. The first six runes of the warning demonstrate the whole ordinary mapping:

	Input rune	Index c	28 − c	Output label

	ᚱ R	4	24	A

	ᛝ NG	21	7	W

	ᚱ R	4	24	A

	ᚪ A	24	4	R

	ᛗ M	19	9	N

	ᚹ W	7	21	NG


With the source separator retained, these produce A-WARNNG. The final NG is one rune label, not two separately decoded symbols. The contextual heading “A warning” is a reading decision; adding an I to the cipher output would change the literal result. Compare the complete warning and the transliteration conventions.

Reverse, then add the shift

The first koan adds 3 after reversing the alphabet. Its first five indices are 7, 26, 28, 7, 22. The ordinary reversal gives 21, 2, 0, 21, 6; adding 3 gives 24, 5, 3, 24, 9. Those labels read A-COAN with the original separator. See the complete first koan.

One rune through the shifted mapping
Read W: input index 7.
Reverse: 28 − 7 = 21.
Add 3: 21 + 3 = 24.
Read A: output index 24.
If the result passes 28, wrap it using modulo 29. For input 0, the intermediate result 31 wraps to 2.

Changing the order changes the cipher. Adding 3 to input 7 first, then reversing, gives 28 − (7 + 3) = 18, or E—not A. Record the formula rather than only saying “Atbash plus three.” The documented convention is (28 − c + 3) % 29.

Why applying it twice works

Ordinary Atbash undoes itself because 28 − (28 − c) = c. The shifted version also undoes itself when the same shift is used both times. If f(c) = (28 − c + s) mod 29, then the two copies of 28 and the two copies of s cancel in f(f(c)), leaving c modulo 29. This makes a useful implementation check, but does not by itself show that a page uses the cipher.

Some symbols map to themselves. Ordinary Atbash leaves index 14 (X) unchanged. The koan’s shift of 3 leaves index 1 (U) unchanged: (28 − 1 + 3) mod 29 = 1. These are normal applications of the formula, not instructions to skip a rune. In a reproduction trace their copied field remains false. Compare the explicitly recorded exceptions in Vigenère.

The complete ordinary mapping

[Image: Complete ordinary Atbash pairs: 0 F with 28 EA; 1 U with 27 IA; 2 TH with 26 Y; 3 O with 25 AE; 4 R with 24 A; 5 C with 23 D; 6 G with 22 OE; 7 W with 21 NG; 8 H with 20 L; 9 N with 19 M; 10 I with 18 E; 11 J with 17 B; 12 EO with 16 T; 13 P with 15 S; 14 X with itself.]
Fourteen exchanged pairs and one fixed symbol. Each arrow works in both directions. A multi-letter label still names one rune. Download the SVG chart.

This chart covers ordinary Atbash only. The first koan’s additional shift changes its pairs. To redraw the chart from the published alphabet, use the reference-data bundle and run:

python scripts/plot_atbash_pairs.py --output my-atbash-pairs.svg

The chart script uses Python’s standard library, reads data/index.json, and refuses to replace an existing output. It makes no network or AI request.

Try the mapping without any files

This Python 3 example checks all 29 input indices for both documented variants, then prints the two heading fragments. No package installation or manuscript download is needed for this small arithmetic check.

labels = "F U TH O R C G W H N I J EO P X S T B E M L NG OE D A AE Y IA EA".split()

def atbash(c, shift=0):
    return (28 - c + shift) % 29

for shift in (0, 3):
    assert sorted(atbash(c, shift) for c in range(29)) == list(range(29))
    assert all(atbash(atbash(c, shift), shift) == c for c in range(29))

warning = [4, 21, 4, 24, 19, 7]
koan = [7, 26, 28, 7, 22]
print(" ".join(labels[atbash(c)] for c in warning))
print(" ".join(labels[atbash(c, 3)] for c in koan))
# A W A R N NG
# A C O A N

The spaces here separate output rune labels so that the mapping is easy to inspect. To retain the manuscript’s punctuation and line breaks, use the full reproduction script below.

How to replicate
python scripts/reproduce_reading.py warning
python scripts/reproduce_reading.py first-koan
python scripts/reproduce_reading.py warning --trace
The trace exposes each rune’s operation and result. Punctuation remains in place. Compare with the exact controls and known readings.

What passing a control means
A matching output confirms that your convention reproduces that passage. It does not establish that an unsolved page uses Atbash. Keep ordinary and shifted variants distinct in a test record.
Sources and verification
