If an order-n square has row sum M, adding all rows gives a total of nM. Thus the total of all entries divided by n is the only possible common row sum. For this example, the total is 5165, so the candidate is 5165 / 5 = 1033. That is a necessary condition, not a substitute for checking the individual lines.

For a normal square, the sum of the integers 1 through n² is n²(n² + 1) / 2. Dividing by n gives the familiar constant n(n² + 1) / 2. A normal order-5 square therefore has constant 65. Applying that formula to this non-normal historical arrangement would be a category error: it does not contain the integers 1 through 25.

Symmetry is a different property

The three-by-three interior in the signed payload looks balanced because it repeats under horizontal and vertical reflection. But its outer rows total 32 while its middle row totals 38. Its columns likewise total 32, 38, and 32; both main diagonals total 34. The total of all entries is 102, giving a candidate constant of 34, yet not one row reaches that value.

	Check	Historical 5 × 5	Payload interior 3 × 3

	All row sums equal?	Yes: 1033	No: 32, 38, 32

	All column sums equal?	Yes: 1033	No: 32, 38, 32

	Both main diagonals match that sum?	Yes: 1033	Both are 34, but the rows and columns fail

	Magic under the stated definition?	Yes	No


A centered layout, repeated numbers, or matching diagonals can be worth describing without calling the arrangement magic. The LP2-15 panel guide applies this same separation between visible pattern and checked sums to its sixteen printed values.

Sources
Pinned 2014 walkthrough · LP1-10 body · All signed payloads and hashes.


Looking for the letter-and-number arrays between plant borders? See LP2-49–51’s alphanumeric grids. Their rectangular layout alone does not make them magic squares.

title: The LP2-56 hash target
summary: The exact printed value, its representation, and the assumptions a candidate check must state.
text:
LP2-56 has a known reading titled “An End.” Its text refers to a page in the deep web that hashes to the hexadecimal value printed between the runic passages. Decoding the surrounding runes and finding the referenced page are separate tasks.

The page record separates the printed hexadecimal block from the runic passages and red punctuation. Five large black dots sit below the text; the illustrated dot guide records them independently of the hash.
The literal target
The archived transcription preserves five printed rows:
36367763ab73783c7af284446c
59466b4cd653239a311cb7116
d4618dee09a8425893dc7500b
464fdaf1672d7bef5e891c6e227
4568926a49fb4f45132c2a8b4
Concatenating the rows yields 128 hexadecimal characters, representing 64 bytes, or 512 bits. The rows are presentation breaks; preserving them in a text file is different from the single digest string used for comparison.

Length is evidence of format, not proof of an algorithm
A SHA-512 digest has this length. The quoted decoded instruction does not name SHA-512 or define which bytes of a “page” should be hashed. Length alone cannot distinguish all algorithms that produce 512-bit outputs. State SHA-512 explicitly as an assumption when testing a candidate.
A URL string, an HTTP response body, an HTML source file, rendered text, and a screenshot are different inputs. Their hashes need not agree. Encoding, line endings, compression handling, and trailing newlines also matter. Do not silently normalize a candidate after a mismatch.

Extract the target from the shipped reading
import json, re
from pathlib import Path
page = json.loads(Path("data/pages/lp2-56.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
lines = [line.rstrip("/") for line in page["reading"]["literal"].splitlines()]
rows = [line for line in lines if re.fullmatch(r"[0-9a-f]+", line)]
target = "".join(rows)
assert len(rows) == 5 and len(target) == 128
assert len(bytes.fromhex(target)) == 64
print(target)
This extracts a preserved target. It does not discover a destination, query a network, or test candidate pages. Use the reading recipe to reproduce the surrounding text independently.

Compare a local candidate file
The candidate-file checker makes one explicit assumption: SHA-512 is the algorithm to test. It reads an existing local file as bytes, without parsing HTML, decoding text, changing line endings, or making a network request.
Extract the reference-data bundle and run from that folder, replacing the quoted path with the file you want to check:
python scripts/check_lp2_target.py "candidate.html"
The JSON report includes the file’s byte count, SHA-256 for identifying the tested bytes, computed SHA-512, preserved target digest, and matches. It also records the hash of the page record from which the target was extracted. The script reads the candidate and prints the report; it does not modify either source file.
	Exit status	Meaning
	0	The computed SHA-512 equals the target.
	1	The exact tested bytes do not match under SHA-512.
	2	The input could not be read or the target record was invalid; no comparison result was produced.
An exit status of 1 is an ordinary mismatch, not a script malfunction. A report identifies what was hashed, but cannot supply missing provenance: record where the candidate came from, when it was obtained, and how it was saved. A browser’s saved HTML and a captured response body may contain different bytes even when they display similarly.
Record exactly what a candidate check establishes
A mismatch excludes the tested bytes under the chosen algorithm. It does not exclude every version of a site, every serialization, or every algorithm. A reported match should include the exact candidate bytes, their provenance, the hashing operation, and an independently repeatable comparison. See checksums and reproducibility.

Sources and status
Original image and reading · Structured record · Pinned walkthrough. The source snapshot establishes the known reading; this article does not assert that the referenced page has been located.

title: The LP2-15 number panel and heading
summary: The exact 4 × 4 matrix, checked totals, red entry, heading, and open-loop drawing.
text:
LP2-15 contains a red runic heading, a 4 × 4 decimal panel, and an open-loop drawing below it. Its combined archive index is 32. Use the release ID when citing it: LP1-15 is a different image with a known keyed reading.

[Image: Detail of LP2-15 showing the red runic heading, all sixteen numbers and the crossed-loop drawing]
Cropped view of LP2-15, retaining the page’s orientation and colors. Compare the four rows with the transcription below; the complete sheet remains available in the original file. Complete original JPEG · Download
The exact number panel
Values in image order; row and column positions are one-based here.
	Row	Column 1	Column 2	Column 3	Column 4

	1	3258	3222	3152	3038

	2	3278	3299 (red)	3298	2838

	3	3288	3294	3296	2472

	4	4516	1206	708	1820

3299 is the only red number. 708 is the only three-digit entry. Preserve 4516 as printed; its being larger than 3301 is not a reason to change it. The structured page record stores the matrix in its numbers field.

Straightforward arithmetic
The row sums are 12670, 12713, 12350, and 8250. The column sums are 14340, 11021, 10454, and 10168. The two main diagonals sum to 11673 and 14146. All sixteen entries sum to 45983.
These unequal totals mean that the printed panel is not a magic square under the ordinary equal-line-sums definition. This says nothing about a proposed transformation of the entries; a transformed panel would be a different object and require its own stated rule.

Subtracting the entries from 3301

Choose the explicit operation d = 3301 − printed entry, keeping all sixteen positions. The resulting panel is:

Derived differences, not numbers printed on the page
	Row	Column 1	Column 2	Column 3	Column 4

	1	43	79	149	263

	2	23	2	3	463

	3	13	7	5	829

	4	−1215	2095	2593	1481


Fourteen differences are prime. All twelve entries in the first three rows are prime, as are the final two entries of the fourth row. The exceptions are 3301 − 4516 = −1215, which is negative and therefore not prime, and 3301 − 1206 = 2095 = 5 × 419, which is composite.

The red 3299 gives a difference of 2, the first prime. The entry 2838 gives 463; separately, 3299 is the 463rd prime. These are checkable numerical relationships. They do not establish that the page instructs either subtraction or an ordinal lookup. See the two directions of a prime lookup.

Using an absolute value, changing a printed entry, or dropping the last row would define a different procedure. Keep the full panel when describing this one. Counting fourteen primes is a descriptive result; judging how surprising it is requires a stated comparison model and an account of how the constant and operation were selected.

Download all sixteen positions as CSV · Download the matrix and checks as JSON. The CSV keeps the printed value and derived difference in separate columns. Row and column coordinates start at one in the image’s original orientation; difference_is_prime is explicitly true or false. Each row also records the operation and source hashes. Sort entire rows to keep those fields together.

Reproduce the difference panel

python scripts/check_number_examples.py

The output’s lp2_15 object includes the source-record hash, original-image hash, printed matrix, transformed matrix and a Boolean prime flag for each position. Primality is checked by exact trial division through the integer square root. Run from the repository or extracted reference-data bundle with Python 3. The script reads the stored panel and does not modify it or execute a cipher search.

The heading is not a known plaintext
[Image: Red LP2-15 heading with dot clusters at either end and a separator between its two rune groups]
Heading detail from the original image. The terminal dot clusters and the separator between groups are visible alongside the runes. Complete original JPEG · Download
The recorded heading has nine runes in groups of four and five: F U L M / A EA Y OE A. EA and OE each label a single rune. These are transliteration labels, not an English translation. The source snapshot does not establish “CRYING” or another plaintext for this heading.

The drawing below the panel
[Image: Black two-lobed drawing beneath the LP2-15 number panel, with two open ends near the center]
Drawing detail from the original image. Inspect the open ends near the center rather than substituting a typeset infinity symbol. Complete original JPEG · Download
The page annotation describes two open lobes with a crossing, resembling an infinity sign; visible gaps remain. Shape resemblance does not establish that the author intended a particular Unicode character, its code point, or a numerical transformation of that code point. Keep the observed drawing separate from those proposed operations.

How to reproduce the totals
import json
from pathlib import Path
p = json.loads(Path("data/pages/lp2-15.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
a = p["numbers"]
assert len(a) == 4 and all(len(row) == 4 for row in a)
print("rows", [sum(row) for row in a])
print("columns", [sum(row[c] for row in a) for c in range(4)])
print("diagonals", sum(a[i][i] for i in range(4)),
      sum(a[i][3-i] for i in range(4)))
print("total", sum(map(sum, a)))
This is a check of the published transcription, not a cipher experiment or a new image audit. Compare the matrix to the original in the reader before using it as an input.

Following a numerical idea
The prime-index guide checks the arithmetic involving 3299, 30557, 9467, and 98597. The emirp guide distinguishes decimal reversal from mirroring and unspecified “inversion.” A valid calculation does not by itself connect LP2-15 with LP2-00–02. Record that proposed connection as a hypothesis with explicit operations and scope.

Sources
Original image, annotations, and archive provenance · Pinned number and rune transcription. Visual observations follow the existing page annotations; the totals above are derived arithmetic.


See also: illustrated index · dots and punctuation · Möbius and the crossed loop.

title: The two LP1 title pages
summary: Visible Latin headings, the meaning of Intus, and the hidden-message chain.
text:
Looking for the cover with compasses? See the illustrated cover and its Blake artwork. It is separate from the title pages discussed here.

The first release includes two title images among its seventeen pages. They are part of the file sequence and the hidden-message chain, even though neither has a runic paragraph.


[Image: Cropped preview of the Latin title Liber Primus on LP1-00]
LP1-00 · Liber Primus. Preview of the visible lettering; open the reader to inspect the complete page and margins.

[Image: Cropped preview showing Chapter 1 above Intus on LP1-02]
LP1-02 · Chapter 1 — Intus. The gap between the two text groups is visible in this preview.


These cropped previews help identify the pages; they are not the files used for OutGuess extraction. Use the LP1-00 original download and LP1-02 original download for byte-level work.

LP1-00: Liber Primus
The cover displays “Liber Primus” in large black Latin lettering on a white field. The text sits above the vertical midpoint with broad margins. The literal visible text is recorded separately from the archived rune transcriptions; a rune count of zero does not mean the image contains no text or no information.

LP1-02: Chapter 1 — Intus
The chapter title displays “Chapter 1” above “Intus,” in black Latin lettering on white. The two text groups are vertically separated. In Latin, intus can mean “within” or “on the inside”; see the Lewis and Short dictionary entry. That lexical meaning does not by itself specify a cipher operation.

Both carry hidden messages
Each original JPEG yields a signed hexadecimal OutGuess body. Together with the warning image, LP1-01, they form the three-image XOR and transposition chain. Their visible headings and embedded bodies must remain separate in transcriptions and citations.

How to inspect the layers
Open the original image in the reader and compare its visible lettering with the labeled visible-text transcription.
Download the original JPEG, not the cropped thumbnail.
Follow OutGuess extraction and compare the expected checksum.
Verify the signed block, then follow the documented three-image chain.
The site’s title-page text is a labeled editorial transcription checked against the image on 19 October 2026. It is not a new cipher reading or a replacement for the image.

Sources
LP1-00 original and file provenance · LP1-02 original and file provenance · Hidden-payload evidence. Visual descriptions concern the displayed originals; no font identification or numerical interpretation of the layout is asserted.

title: The image hidden in LP1-03
summary: The decoded JPEG, its archived rune transcription, and exact reproduction steps.
text:
LP1-03 has two different images to examine: the visible runic manuscript page and a smaller JPEG encoded inside its signed OutGuess message. The known Vigenère reading of the manuscript does not automatically decode the second image.

Four layers to keep separate

	Layer	What you examine
	Original LP1-03 JPEG	The visible Welcome page, with its runes and leafy border. It also carries hidden data.
	OutGuess payload	31,809 extracted bytes containing the signed message.
	Signed message body	A short instruction followed by hexadecimal text representing another JPEG.
	Decoded JPEG	The small rune-and-digit image shown below, 15,188 bytes long.

The body opens with “Let the text guide you.”, then “Good luck.” and “3301”, before the hexadecimal sequence. These words are in the extracted message, not the visible runic paragraph on the manuscript sheet. Read the complete body or inspect the signed block.

OutGuess extraction, signature verification, and hexadecimal decoding answer different questions. Extraction retrieves the stored bytes. Signature verification checks the signed content against a particular public key. Hexadecimal decoding converts character pairs into bytes. None of those operations alone supplies a reading of the runes in the resulting image.

The decoded derivative
[Image: A narrow black rune sequence containing the decimal digits 5 and 3 on a white background]
The JPEG decoded from the hexadecimal portion of LP1-03’s signed message.
The derivative is 587 × 109 pixels and 15,188 bytes. Download the JPEG. Its checksum is recorded in the payload manifest.

Archived transcription
The pinned iBotPeaches archive supplies this transcription:
ᚦᛗᛞᛇᚠᛗᚪᚱ5ᚢᚫᛝᚱᛝ3 ᛠᛗᛇᚠᛡ
It contains 18 runes and the decimal digits 5 and 3. In the wiki’s alphabet labels, with spaces inserted between individual symbols for clarity:
TH M D EO F M A R 5 U AE NG R NG 3 EA M EO F IA
Those labels are a transliteration, not established plaintext. The added spaces above identify symbol boundaries; they are not a new claim about word boundaries in the image. Decimal digits remain digits rather than becoming rune indices.

How to reproduce the image
First follow OutGuess extraction for LP1-03 and verify its signed message. Decode the hexadecimal suffix of the exported body:
import hashlib
import json
from pathlib import Path

manifest = json.loads(
    Path("data/evidence/embedded-payloads.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
)
record = next(row for row in manifest["records"] if row["page"] == "lp1-03")
body_bytes = Path(record["body_path"]).read_bytes()
if hashlib.sha256(body_bytes).hexdigest() != record["body_sha256"]:
    raise ValueError("Message body differs from the recorded source")
body = body_bytes.decode("utf-8")
image = bytes.fromhex(body[body.index("ffd8ffe"):])
if len(image) != record["embedded_image_bytes"]:
    raise ValueError("Decoded JPEG length differs from the record")
if hashlib.sha256(image).hexdigest() != record["embedded_image_sha256"]:
    raise ValueError("Decoded JPEG differs from the recorded derivative")
with open("lp1-03-decoded.jpg", "xb") as output:
    output.write(image)
print("Verified and wrote", len(image), "bytes")
The exclusive-create mode refuses to overwrite an existing file. This reproduces a format conversion, not a proposed solution to the image’s text. Keep the original signed body and the derivative as separate files.

Run the example from an extracted reference-data bundle or the repository root. It uses only Python’s standard library. A successful run prints Verified and wrote 15188 bytes. The hashes check consistency with the supplied manifest; authenticate the signed message separately using the linked verification instructions.
If a hash check fails, stop before interpreting the derivative. Confirm that the message body and manifest come from the same download, and avoid opening and resaving the body in an editor that changes line endings. Use the file-verification guide to compare bytes. The checks deliberately read the body as bytes before decoding its text.
Sources
Pinned transcription of the embedded image · Signed block · Message body · Payload inventory.

title: LP2-00–02: text and image measurements
summary: Cross-like margin drawings, loops, the insect, and measured rune and punctuation regions on the opening pages.
text:
LP2-00, LP2-01, and LP2-02 are the first three images of the second release. Their combined archive indices are 17–19. The source snapshot does not give them a known plaintext. Studying them together does not establish a shared key or a reset rule.

[Image: LP2-00 manuscript preview]
LP2-00 · Read
[Image: LP2-01 manuscript preview]
LP2-01 · Read
[Image: LP2-02 manuscript preview]
LP2-02 · Read
Crosses, loops, and the insect

All three pages place one cross-like drawing high in the right margin and another lower in the left margin. Each has a long stem crossed by three bars. The broadest bar is near the upper end of the right-hand drawing and the lower end of the left-hand drawing. This makes the pair useful to compare, but visual resemblance alone does not establish that one is an exact rotation of the other.

	Page	Beyond the margin drawings	Inspect

	LP2-00	Small two-lobed loops above and below the text.	Page 00 notes

	LP2-01	A loop above the text, without a corresponding loop below the final row.	Page 01 notes

	LP2-02	A winged insect-like drawing below the text, with its head to the right and a striped wing extending left.	Page 02 notes


The labels “cross,” “signpost,” and “infinity” describe resemblances. They do not settle a religious identification, a direction to read the runes, or an arithmetic operation. For comparison with other pages, see insect imagery and the larger crossed loop on LP2-15. A proposed connection should identify the exact drawings and what feature is being compared.

What has been measured
	Page	Rune regions	Red runes	Dark runes	Punctuation regions

	LP2-00	262	13	249	58

	LP2-01	266	0	266	62

	LP2-02	201	0	201	38

These are 729 stored rune regions and 158 punctuation regions. A region is a measurement unit, not necessarily a separate linguistic character. Rune counts refer to the archived transcription and its mapped image regions.

Punctuation has its own color and shape
LP2-00 has 56 one-component punctuation regions, one four-component region, and one thirteen-component region. One of its one-component marks and its thirteen-component mark are classified red. LP2-01 has 57 one-component and five four-component regions, all dark. LP2-02 has 36 one-component regions, one four-component region, and one thirteen-component region; the thirteen-component region is red.
Thus LP2-02 has no red rune regions but does have red punctuation. The recorded component count describes connected foreground pixels under a threshold, not the number of sentences, cipher shifts, or semantic separators. See image regions and connected components.

Layout details that affect inspection
LP2-00’s oversized opening S rune extends alongside the first three text rows. Its stored rectangle is [599, 664, 153, 501] in original-image pixels. Treating each horizontal row as independent can miss that shared visual context.
LP2-01’s recorded tenth visual row contains C/OE glyphs touching at their feet. Overlapping inspection rectangles preserve their context. A touching shape does not automatically merge the two transcription symbols.

Do not equate transcript punctuation with pixel shape
The archived ASCII notation can use the same period character for marks with different visual component counts. A period in exported text therefore does not prove that every corresponding mark has the same appearance. Keep transcription conventions, image observations, and a proposed reset rule separate.

How to inspect and reproduce the inventory
Open a page record and expand its recorded rune or punctuation regions.
Select “Inspect region” to view the recorded rectangle against the original image.
Use the page JSON’s visual.glyphs and visual.punctuation arrays to inspect the stored data.
Run the checks below from the repository root.
# Structural checks and stored counts; Python standard library:
python scripts/inspect_visual_records.py
# Fresh color/component recount within stored rectangles; requires Pillow:
python scripts/inspect_visual_records.py --pixels
If Pillow is not installed, install it with python -m pip install Pillow in your chosen Python environment. The pixel check verifies the original JPEG hashes before reading them. It does not generate new segmentation, decide which rune a shape represents, or test a cipher.

Evidence and limits
Measurement conventions and checked scope · Reproduction script · LP2-00 source record · LP2-01 source record · LP2-02 source record. Color classes and component counts were reproduced inside the published rectangles on 19 October 2026. This does not make the visual inventory exhaustive or establish a relationship with LP2-15’s number panel.


See also: illustrated index · dots and punctuation · Möbius and the crossed loop.

title: Image regions and connected components
summary: Understand pixel rectangles, thresholded shapes, and recorded color classes.
text:
An image region specifies where a measurement was made. Keeping the rectangle, original image, and measurement rule together lets another person inspect the same pixels.

Reading a rectangle
The wiki uses [x, y, width, height] in original-image pixels. The origin is the top-left; x increases rightward and y downward. For [599, 664, 153, 501], the region starts at x = 599, y = 664 and covers 153 columns and 501 rows. In a half-open crop convention, the right and bottom bounds are 752 and 1165.
A thumbnail or resized preview uses different display coordinates. Use the original JPEG or the wiki’s region inspector rather than copying screen coordinates into a dataset.

Connected components
A connected component is a group of selected pixels joined by the chosen neighborhood rule. Eight-connectivity includes horizontal, vertical, and diagonal neighbors. Four-connectivity excludes diagonal neighbors; the same image can produce different counts under those definitions.
The published opening-page measurement uses foreground grayscale below 140 and retains eight-connected groups containing at least 20 pixels. Tiny isolated specks are excluded by that area threshold. A count of 13 means thirteen qualifying groups under this rule, not necessarily thirteen intentional dots.

The same pixels, two different counts

In this invented three-by-three mask, # marks a selected foreground pixel and . marks background. It is a teaching example, not a manuscript crop.

# . .
. # .
. . #

	Neighborhood rule	Connections in this mask	Components

	Four-connected	Only shared horizontal or vertical edges count. None of the selected pixels share an edge.	3 components, each of area 1

	Eight-connected	Corner neighbors also connect. The middle pixel connects both outer pixels.	1 component of area 3


Connectivity is transitive: the two outer pixels need not touch each other to belong to the same group. A path through the middle pixel is enough. This is why a thin diagonal bridge can merge what a person sees as separate marks.

Reproduce the small mask

This Python 3 example counts all selected pixels, with no minimum-area filter. It needs no image package:

def component_areas(points, diagonal=False):
    remaining = set(points)
    neighbors = [(1, 0), (-1, 0), (0, 1), (0, -1)]
    if diagonal:
        neighbors += [(1, 1), (1, -1), (-1, 1), (-1, -1)]
    areas = []
    while remaining:
        pending = [remaining.pop()]
        area = 0
        while pending:
            x, y = pending.pop()
            area += 1
            for dx, dy in neighbors:
                neighbor = (x + dx, y + dy)
                if neighbor in remaining:
                    remaining.remove(neighbor)
                    pending.append(neighbor)
        areas.append(area)
    return sorted(areas)

pixels = {(0, 0), (1, 1), (2, 2)}
assert component_areas(pixels) == [1, 1, 1]
assert component_areas(pixels, diagonal=True) == [3]
assert component_areas(set()) == []
print("Four-connected:", component_areas(pixels))
print("Eight-connected:", component_areas(pixels, diagonal=True))

Each selected pixel is removed from the remaining set when it is assigned to a component, so it cannot be counted twice. The reported areas total three under either rule. Connectivity changes grouping, not how many foreground pixels exist.

The real opening-page rule additionally discards components smaller than 20 pixels. Applied to this tiny teaching mask, that filter would retain zero components under either connectivity rule. Always report the neighborhood, brightness threshold and minimum area together; “three dots” is not a complete measurement specification.

Measure the five dots on LP2-56

The five isolated dots below the hash-target text provide a manageable first measurement. The rectangle [800, 2350, 900, 500] contains the dots without the writing above them. Its coordinates refer to the original 2400 by 3600 pixel image.

Download and extract both the reference data and original images into the same directory. Run these commands there, with Python 3 installed:

python -m pip install Pillow
python scripts/measure_region.py lp2-56 --rect 800 2350 900 500 --threshold 140 --minimum-area 20 --connectivity 8

The script checks the original JPEG against the page record’s SHA-256 before decoding it. It converts the pixels to grayscale with Pillow, selects values strictly below 140, groups eight-connected neighbors, and discards groups smaller than 20 pixels. It prints JSON and leaves the image unchanged.

Expected result

With Pillow 11.3.0, the region contains 17,888 selected pixels in five retained components; no small components are discarded. The table lists them from top to bottom by centroid. These row numbers are measurement labels, not a proposed reading order.

	Component	Area in pixels	Centroid (x, y)
	1	3559	1103.934, 2447.301
	2	3560	873.346, 2517.000
	3	3604	1603.870, 2686.500
	4	3542	921.227, 2708.059
	5	3623	1408.122, 2747.286

A centroid is the arithmetic mean of the selected pixels’ x and y indices. It estimates the center of this dark pixel group, not an intended geometric point. The table rounds to three decimal places for readability; the complete JSON result retains six decimals, bounding rectangles, input hash, Pillow version and all measurement settings.

To measure another region, change the page ID and rectangle. Keep the output with your notes, including any settings you change. A rectangle that cuts through a dot measures only the retained part; a threshold that admits a connecting stroke can merge groups. Comparing two patterns also requires a stated rule for matching points and allowing translation, rotation or scaling. Five components alone establish none of those relationships.

Color classification
Within a stored rectangle, foreground pixels use the weighted brightness test 0.299R + 0.587G + 0.114B < 140. A foreground pixel is red-dominant when R − max(G,B) > 70. A red-dominant fraction above 90% gives “red”; below 10% gives “dark”; intermediate cases are “mixed/uncertain.” These labels summarize pixels under a rule, not a chemical analysis of ink.

What a successful recount establishes
Matching a recorded count confirms that the stated operation reproduces it on the stored rectangle and exact image bytes. It does not prove that the rectangle includes every relevant mark or that two overlapping rectangles should be interpreted as one character. Segmentation, symbol identification, and cipher interpretation are separate decisions.

Reproduce the published examples
Follow the LP2-00–02 inventory and run python scripts/inspect_visual_records.py --pixels. The measurement manifest records the scope and input hashes; the script shows the exact implementation. Keep file integrity separate from a claim about meaning.

title: Reproducing rune prime sums
summary: Compute exact sentence and word totals, test explicit spelling changes, and keep arithmetic separate from intent.
text:
A prime-sum claim is a claim about a particular sequence of runes under a particular counting rule. Before asking why a spelling was chosen, establish which text was counted and whether the claimed total can be reproduced. The spelling reference discusses individual cases; this guide walks through the calculation.

Choose the input layer

The page record’s ordinary prime sum describes its archived runes. For an encrypted page, this is a ciphertext sum. The examples here instead use the known decoded rune sequence, with the documented correction and cipher rules applied. These are different quantities even when both are called “the page sum.”

Use the rune’s Gematria Primus prime value, not its zero-based cipher index. Count each rune once. The rule here excludes spaces, punctuation, line-wrap markers and printed decimal numbers. A Latin label such as IA or NG denotes one rune; it must not automatically become two individual letter-runes.

Reproduce the sum displayed on a page

The metadata beside each manuscript image reports the archived rune count and prime sum. For LP2-31, these are 269 runes and 13,680. They describe the encrypted transcription, not a proposed plaintext.

Use this Python 3 example from the repository root or extracted reference-data bundle. Change page_id to another page with an archived rune transcription. The script reads the archive text, looks up each rune’s prime value, and checks both results against the page record:

import json
from pathlib import Path

page_id = "lp2-31"
index = json.loads(Path("data/index.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
primes = {item["rune"]: item["prime"] for item in index["alphabet"]}
text = Path(f"text/{page_id}.txt").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
unknown = {char for char in text if "\u16a0" <= char <= "\u16ff"} - primes.keys()
if unknown:
    raise ValueError(f"Unknown runic symbols: {unknown}")
values = [primes[char] for char in text if char in primes]
page = json.loads(Path(f"data/pages/{page_id}.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
if len(values) != page["rune_count"] or sum(values) != page["prime_sum"]:
    raise ValueError("Calculated values differ from the page record")
print("Archived runes:", len(values))
print("Archived prime sum:", sum(values))

Expected output:
Archived runes: 269
Archived prime sum: 13680

Only recognized rune symbols contribute. Archive delimiters, line endings and decimal digits do not. Unknown characters within the Unicode Runic block cause an error instead of silently disappearing. This checks the published metadata against its transcription and alphabet; it is not an independent verification of the image transcription.

A sum preserves no ordering information: rearranging the same runes gives the same total. Matching 13,680 therefore cannot establish that two transcriptions are identical or that a rearrangement is correct. Use the exact source file and its checksum to identify the input; use cipher invariants to understand which transformations can change the statistic. The first-row example explains why Latin-letter counts differ from rune counts.

Run the read-only check

python scripts/reproduce_prime_sums.py
python scripts/reproduce_prime_sums.py --json

Run from the repository or the extracted reference-data ZIP using Python 3. See script setup if this is your first command. The first prints a concise report. The second prints the full rune sequences, prime values, totals and counterfactual results as JSON. Neither command changes files, accesses the network, or calls an AI.

The script re-decodes the nine documented controls, verifies all 17 literal page readings, reconstructs the rune stream from the per-rune trace, and compares the ten selected word occurrences and four LP2-57 segments with the published arithmetic evidence. The ten occurrences are the examples selected for the spelling article, not an exhaustive sample of all manuscript words. This shares the known-reading implementation; it is not an independent photographic transcription.

The same page before and after decoding

A known decoding can preserve the number of runes while changing their prime sum. Compare the Warning on LP1-01 with the parable on LP2-57:

	Page and method	Runes	Archived sum	Decoded sum
	LP1-01 · Atbash	184	11,417	7,409
	LP2-57 · Direct reading	95	3,968	3,968

Atbash replaces each rune index x with 28 − x. There is still one output rune per input rune, but the replacement rune generally has a different Gematria Primus value. Summing those replacement values gives 7,409, a difference of −4,008. Do not subtract the archived sum from a constant: Atbash acts on each alphabet index, not on the page’s accumulated prime values.

LP2-57 uses the same rune sequence for its direct reading, so its total does not change. Both totals in that row include the heading and the body. The sentence sums below use smaller boundaries and answer a different question.

Run python scripts/reproduce_prime_sums.py --json and find page_sums. It reports the archived and decoded totals, their difference, the rune count and the archived transcription’s SHA-256 for every known-reading page. The script re-decodes and checks the literal controls before calculating these comparisons.

Download the comparison
All 17 page comparisons are available as CSV for a spreadsheet or JSON with scope and reproduction command. Both include the exact archived transcription hash for each row. The difference column is decoded minus archived; it is not a change in rune count. These files are also included in the reference-data bundle.
A changed sum is not a decoding score. Correct substitutions may change it, while arbitrary rearrangements preserve it. Establish the method against the known controls, and keep preserved statistics separate from evidence that an output is meaningful.

LP2-57: boundaries change the claim

For LP2-57, remove archive line-wrap markers and divide at the archive’s periods. This gives a heading followed by three body segments:

	Segment	Sum	Reversal	Result
	PARABLE heading	449	944	Prime sum, composite reversal
	First body sentence	1259	9521	Emirp
	Second body sentence	1031	1301	Emirp
	Third body sentence	1229	9221	Emirp

An emirp must be prime, and its decimal reversal must be a different prime. Combining heading and body gives 449 + 1259 + 1031 + 1229 = 3968, which is even and greater than 2, hence composite. Including the heading therefore changes the proposition from three emirp sentence sums to a composite page total. There is no contradiction: the boundaries differ.

What does a spelling change actually do?

Start with the exact original sequence, specify an alternate sequence, and subtract their totals. For a replacement of one rune by several, the change is the sum of the inserted rune values minus the removed rune value.

Worked example: CWESTIAN

The second word of the Instruction reading on LP1-16 contains seven runes. In the labels used by the arithmetic evidence, they are C, W, E, S, T, IA and N. The final three Latin letters in “TIAN” therefore do not represent three separate runes: IA is one alphabet entry worth 107.

C    W    E    S    T    IA    N
13 + 19 + 67 + 53 + 59 + 107 + 29 = 347

Reverse the decimal digits: 347 → 743
Both are prime, and they are different: 347 is an emirp.

Now construct an alternative that represents the sound with separate I and O runes. Keep every other rune fixed. Their combined value is 31 + 7 = 38, so replacing 107 with 38 gives 347 − 107 + 38 = 278. This is a real arithmetic difference. Writing the original rune’s label as IO instead of IA, or C as K, would leave the underlying seven runes and their sum unchanged. See transliteration conventions before comparing Latin spellings.

Compare the other cases

TUNNELNG → a separate I before NG: adding I contributes 31. The first LP2-57 sentence changes from 1259 to 1290. The alternate total is composite. NG/ING is a multi-letter rune convention, so this comparison does not establish that the original is a spelling error.

CWESTIAN with one IA/IO rune → separate I and O: remove 107 and add 31 + 7. The change is −69; the word total becomes 347 − 69 = 278, composite. Simply relabeling C as K or IA as IO changes no rune and therefore no sum.

WIDSOM → WISDOM: exchanging D and S changes no values or multiplicities. The total remains 270. A reordering cannot make this additive total prime.

BELIEUE ↔ BELEIUE: exchanging I and E also preserves the total, 369. The documented transcription correction is important for source fidelity and order-sensitive ciphers; it does not tune the additive sum.

These alternatives are explicitly constructed comparisons. They are not additional text found on the manuscript.

A quick arithmetic check

Only the F rune has the even prime value 2; every other rune value is odd. The sum is odd exactly when the number of non-F runes is odd. An even total greater than 2 cannot be prime. This provides a quick necessary check before trial division, not a sufficient test: many odd totals are composite.

Adding I flips parity because 31 is odd. Reordering a word cannot change parity or any other property of its additive total. Keeping those invariants explicit helps distinguish a meaningful numerical change from a visually different spelling with identical arithmetic.

What this says about purpose

For the manuscript’s philosophical use of the term, see primality and divinity. A prime-valued alphabet provides numerical context, but does not by itself specify which sums the prose asks a reader to calculate.

The reproducible observation is that the three body sums are emirps under the declared convention. The counterfactuals show that some alternate encodings lose a property, while reorderings and aliases do not affect it. Neither statement alone identifies the author’s reason for choosing a spelling.

Could a prime sum act as a consistency check?

That is one possible purpose: if a reader knew in advance that each sentence should have an emirp sum, a sentence with a composite sum would signal a mismatch with that rule. The reader could then check the transcription, rune interpretation and sentence boundary. In the first LP2-57 sentence, inserting a separate I changes 1259 to 1290, so this proposed check would reject that particular insertion.

Passing would be much weaker evidence. “The sum is an emirp” accepts many different totals. Even an exact expected total accepts any rearrangement of the same runes. WIDSOM and WISDOM both total 270: a sum cannot tell which order the manuscript uses. It also loses information beyond order. For example, the synthetic two-rune sequences U–O and TH–TH both total 10: 3 + 7 = 5 + 5. These are different rune collections with the same length and total, not manuscript words or a proposed reading.

A useful check therefore needs an independently justified expectation, not just a property discovered after trying different boundaries. It can help reject some candidate transcriptions; it cannot recover the wording by itself. Compare what cipher operations preserve and file checksums, which address a different question: whether the file bytes match a specified reference.

A proposed purpose such as marking sentence boundaries or providing a consistency check needs a separately stated rule and a complete set of cases. It should explain which units are meant to satisfy the rule and which choices were allowed. Selecting only successful words, or adding a delimiter value after seeing a composite total, changes the test. See selection effects and reproducible scope. This guide does not assign a probability that the observed totals were intentional.

Sources and verification

Read-only reproduction script · Known-reading implementation · Method parameters · Exact sum evidence · Complete LP2-57 reading. The calculations and trace reconstruction were checked on 19 October 2026. Successful verification supports the declared arithmetic and recorded inputs; it does not validate every glyph against the original image or establish a new decryption.

The LP1-05 opposite-cell comparison gives concrete equal-sum examples: SHADOWS and CABAL both give 341, while the printed tokens differ. It separates symmetry of the converted number grid from symmetry of the original writing.

title: Philosophical themes in Liber Primus
summary: Authority, identity, circumference, attachment and emergence across the known readings.
text:
The known readings connect authority, identity, attachment and transformation. This guide follows those connections within the manuscript. Resemblance to a philosophical tradition is not proof that the authors belonged to it. Reading status follows the 5 October 2026 source snapshot.

A reading route through the ideas

Start with the complete passages, then use the explanations to compare them. This is a suggested route through four recurring questions, not the manuscript’s chapter order or a claim that it teaches one settled system.


What should you trust? Read A Warning alongside the final LP1 instruction. Notice the combination of questioning, inward discovery, and limits on imposing beliefs. Continue with knowledge and authority.

What counts as an identity? Read the first koan, then the second. Track how the first rejects descriptions and the second turns a thought into its own example. The koan guide explains each exchange.

What creates dependence? Read The Loss of Divinity all the way through its advice about wealth. Ask how possession differs from attachment, and why both dogma and reason appear. Use the page map and close reading to locate each claim.

What changes through the inward journey? Compare the Welcome with the final parable. Follow the recurring instar and emergence language, then connect it to circumference and the biological metaphor.


For the mathematical vocabulary, add Some Wisdom and the discussion of sacred arithmetic below. To read in manuscript order instead, use all known readings.

If the historical vocabulary is unfamiliar, use the short explanations of Zen, Rinzai, and Sōtō and transcendentalism around Emerson. Return to the manuscript passages after reading the background; a shared theme is not an attribution.
Keep a comparison another reader can check

For each connection, save the passage and page or section, the exact wording you are comparing, and a separate sentence explaining your interpretation. If you propose an outside source, add its specific passage or image and explain both the matches and differences. The concordance helps find repeated wording; the works index distinguishes documented puzzle sources from possible influences.

Text, interpretation and attribution

The page records preserve literal rune-label readings. Contextual English expands conventions such as U/V and NG/ING; it helps explain sentences but is not the exact sequence to use in a cipher or prime-sum calculation. Compare the transcription layers before drawing conclusions from spelling.

Three claims need different evidence: a phrase occurs in a known reading; two passages can be read together; an outside work was intentionally referenced. The first can be checked against the recorded decoding. The second is interpretation. The third needs a specific verbal or visual match and a defensible source, not just a shared theme.

Testing authority while preserving the book

Testing knowledge, certainty, and authority follows the warning through the later instructions, with manuscript previews and reproducible wording searches. It separates checking a claim, examining an identity, and directing other people.

For an outside text with a documented role in the earlier puzzle, see Emerson’s Self-Reliance. Its book-cipher use and its philosophical resemblance to these passages are separate connections. The close-reading comparisons locate Emerson’s arguments about conformity, consistency, and fortune in the preserved source.

A Warning asks the reader to test knowledge and find truth, yet also forbids alteration of the book's words or numbers. These instructions can be read together: question the message while preserving the object being examined. That reading helps explain why a research edition should show an original beside its corrections rather than silently replace it. It does not prove that archival practice was the author's intended meaning.

The final LP1 instruction returns to questioning and inward discovery, then adds a limit: impose nothing on others. Read alongside LP1-04's instruction to command one's own self, this suggests a distinction between directing oneself and directing other people. These passages are more specific evidence for personal autonomy than a generic label such as “individualist.”

The two koans: names and the inner voice

The dedicated koan guide explains the term, follows each answer in the first dialogue, and examines the second dialogue’s self-reference.

In the first koan, LP1-06–09, a master repeatedly rejects a student's answers to who they are. A name, occupation, species and account of consciousness do not satisfy the question. The exchange turns attention from descriptions of a person toward the act of identifying a self. The text explicitly calls itself a koan; that label alone does not identify a particular historical source, teacher or school.

The second koan, LP1-14–15, shifts the problem to the voice inside the head. The student's thought that they have no such voice becomes the master's example of it. This is a self-referential literary device: the attempted denial supplies the instance. It is not an empirical demonstration that every reader experiences thought in the same way.

Compare both with the Welcome's promised end to self. Does “self” mean the whole person, the descriptions used to identify them, or the narrated identity attacked in the second koan? The manuscript does not supply a formal definition that settles those alternatives.

Sacred arithmetic and the instruction to encrypt

Some Wisdom, LP1-05, makes three short assertions before the instruction “know this” and its arrangement of numbers and words. In contextual English, their sequence is:

The primes are sacred. A class of numbers receives a religious or evaluative description.
The totient function is sacred. The same description is applied to a mathematical function.
All things should be encrypted. The passage shifts from describing what is sacred to prescribing what should be done.

[Image: LP1-05, with the Some Wisdom text above a five-row arrangement of runes and printed numbers]
LP1-05: inspect the statements and the lower arrangement together. The magic-square guide explains the numerical reading of that arrangement separately.

This is an explicit connection between mathematical vocabulary and the book’s value language. It is stronger evidence for that connection than noticing a prime number elsewhere and assigning it a spiritual meaning. But “sacred” is not defined as a numerical test here. A prime is still defined by its divisors; the totient function counts positive integers up to a specified number that are coprime to it. Neither mathematical definition contains a claim about sacredness.

The encryption sentence is also an instruction, not a description of every page’s current encoding. Some Wisdom itself is a direct reading under the recorded rune-label conventions. The sentence therefore cannot serve, by itself, as proof that every readable passage must have another encrypted layer. A proposal for a second layer needs a defined input and operation, just as a proposal for an unsolved page does.

Read this beside primality and divinity: one passage calls primes sacred; another connects losing primality with losing divinity. The shared vocabulary makes an internal comparison worth pursuing. The texts do not state an equation between a person’s divinity and a word’s prime sum, or require applying the totient function to every rune. Those would be additional hypotheses.

To inspect the literal wording, run python scripts/reproduce_reading.py some-wisdom. It retains FUNCTIAN and THNGS, where the contextual English above uses FUNCTION and THINGS. See the rune-label conventions before treating those differences as alterations to the manuscript.

Circumference, primality and divinity

The Loss of Divinity, LP1-10–13, assigns three behaviors to the circumference: consumption, preservation and adherence. It connects consumption and preservation with fear of insufficiency or inability to recover what is lost. Adherence includes following either dogma or reason for the sake of belonging and being right. The target described is therefore not simply religion; the same motive can attach to reason.

The second koan associates the inner voice with circumference. LP2-57's parable asks for the shedding of circumferences and the discovery of divinity within. Reading these occurrences together supports interpreting circumference as a surrounding or limiting aspect of identity. That is a textual interpretation, not a geometrical decoding rule.

The Loss of Divinity also uses “primality.” The primality and divinity guide compares all recorded occurrences and explains the distinction between arithmetic and metaphor. This connects naturally to prime-valued runes and the manuscript's numerical vocabulary, but the word does not establish which numbers to calculate. A numerical hypothesis must still name its input and boundaries; see reproducing prime sums.

Possession and attachment

The section that criticizes consumption and preservation also tells the reader to amass wealth, avoid attachment to possessions and be prepared to destroy them. Calling the passage a simple rejection of material possessions would miss that tension. A closer reading distinguishes possession from dependence on what is possessed. Whether the commands are literal, rhetorical or initiatory is not established by the decoded words alone.

The same section ends by commanding the reader to program mind and reality. The close reading of that instruction considers its position after the account of dependence and explains what the wording leaves unspecified.

For the opening passage’s sequence of losses and its closing instruction, follow pilgrimage, selfhood, and the Welcome.

The inward journey and emergence

The Welcome links going inward with emerging outward and invokes an instar. LP2-57 repeats the instar image, tunneling, the shedding of circumferences and emergence. This repeated vocabulary connects two distant sections more directly than an outside theory does. Compare LP1-04 with LP2-57.

The imagery permits a reading of transformation through inward examination. It does not by itself identify a biological species, a specific ritual, or a cipher key. The language of death and an end to self also belongs to this literary context; the known reading does not establish an operational instruction for a solver.

Outside works: start with a checkable parallel

The referenced works and possible influences index brings together documented book-cipher sources, cover artwork identifications, and literary comparisons, with the status of each connection.

William Blake and The Marriage of Heaven and Hell compares a close verbal parallel in LP1-04 with its external text. This is a more precise starting point than assigning the whole manuscript to a single movement. A possible allusion in one sentence does not automatically identify the source of its artwork, mathematics or other teachings.

The instruction following the first koan also has a possible literary association with Lewis Carroll's impossible-things dialogue. The wording, number and action differ; the comparison is weaker than a close verbal match.

For a closer reading of the three behaviors and the advice about wealth, see consumption, preservation, and adherence.

Sources and further reading

This is a close reading of the compiled known readings, supported by the linked page records and complete-section guides. For reproduction, use Running the reproduction scripts. The connections here are editorial interpretation, not additional decrypted text or authenticated statements of authorial intent.


Follow the recurring term in circumference, identity, and emergence, or use the known-reading concordance to locate a word or phrase yourself.

title: Referenced works and possible influences
summary: Find documented book sources, cover artwork identifications, and literary parallels with their evidence and limits.
text:
Outside works enter this research in several ways. A text used for a book cipher, an identifiable fragment of a painting, and a sentence resembling another author’s words are different kinds of connection. This index explains what has been documented and takes you to the passages, images, and reproduction details.

Where each connection occurs

Start with the location before following a proposed influence. The earlier puzzle route, the illustrated cover, and the numbered manuscript releases are distinct objects.

	Work	Location in the puzzle	What connects them

	Emerson’s Self-Reliance	The 2014 opening message, before the compasses cover.	A reproducible book-cipher lookup yields the historical address of the cover site.

	Blake’s The Marriage of Heaven and Hell	LP1-04, in the Welcome.	A close verbal parallel concerning life and holiness.

	Carroll’s Through the Looking-Glass	LP1-09, the instruction following the first koan.	A possible comparison: four unreasonable actions versus six impossible beliefs.

	Three Blake compositions	The earlier 1033.jpg cover, not the plain LP1 title images.	Published identifications of visual fragments, discussed separately below.


The reader links open original manuscript images. The complete-reading and comparison guides explain the decoding and outside sources. For the corresponding passage in a particular edition, follow the source cited by that guide rather than assuming that page numbers or paragraph counts transfer between editions.

Texts and literary parallels

Emerson: Self-Reliance

Connection: a documented book-cipher source in the earlier 2014 route.

Inspect: the source PDF, the paragraph, sentence, word, and letter counting convention, and the reproduced historical address.

Blake: The Marriage of Heaven and Hell

Connection: a close verbal parallel with the Welcome’s statement about life being holy. Other passages support thematic comparison.

Inspect: the actual wording and its context in both works, including the different uses of circumference.

Carroll: Through the Looking-Glass

Connection: a possible association with the instruction to do four unreasonable things.

Inspect: chapter V’s White Queen dialogue. Compare doing with believing, four with six, and a daily practice with the recollection about breakfast.


Emerson’s role in the earlier route does not prove that every later statement about selfhood comes from Emerson. Likewise, the Carroll comparison is not a quotation match. The linked articles preserve these limits alongside the evidence.

Artwork in the illustrated cover

[Image: The preserved 1033.jpg cover collage with central compasses fragments and narrow side panels]
The 1033.jpg cover belongs to the earlier puzzle route. It is separate from the plain LP1-00 title image.

The cover studies discussed in the linked guides identify fragments of three Blake compositions. Identifying a composition does not necessarily identify the particular impression, photograph, or digital reproduction used in the collage.


Newton
The upper central compasses panel. Compare the hand, instrument, and drawing, retaining the reported reflection.

The Ancient of Days
The lower central panel. Compare the fragment with the frontispiece to Europe: a Prophecy; the guide discusses rotation and the museum record’s qualified identification of the figure.

Nebuchadnezzar
The narrow side strips. Follow the divided figure and the artwork’s biblical subject without treating the title as cover plaintext.


These guides cite the published cover identification and museum descriptions separately. They also explain what to compare in the preserved image. For the visible motifs on the later manuscript pages, use the illustrated page index.

For the character associated with the lower panel, see Urizen: measurement and limits in Blake. That guide separates the figure’s literary background from the identification of a cover fragment.

Daniel and Newton's commentary

Connection: a proposed shared reference behind the cover's three Blake compositions. The cover reading map separates Nebuchadnezzar's story in Daniel 4, the Ancient of Days in Daniel 7, and Newton's writing about prophecy.

Inspect: the linked biblical passages and Newton's own commentary. The historical connections can be checked independently of the further hypothesis that one of these texts is a cipher source.

Jung: The Red Book

Connection: a published proposal comparing the reclining manuscript figures with an image in Jung's work. The comparison is not yet an independently verified source attribution here.

Inspect: the four manuscript locations and their orientations, the reported source-page locators, and the edition and ISBN information. The guide separates the observed drawings from the proposed source.

Terms and traditions are another kind of reference

The manuscript explicitly labels two dialogues as koans. That establishes the label in the known reading; it does not supply a traditional case number, teacher, lineage, or source collection. The koan guide explains the genre and follows the dialogues before considering outside attribution.

Similarly, instar is a biological term used in the Welcome and final parable. Its definition helps explain the analogy, but it does not identify a source book or prove that every insect drawing depicts the same species. Philosophical themes follows connections internal to the manuscript.

How to add a useful comparison

Locate both objects. Give the manuscript ID and the outside work’s edition, chapter, plate, or collection record.
Show the correspondence. Preserve exact wording or specify the matching visual features. Record cropping, rotation, or reflection.
Record differences. A shared subject is less specific than the same arrangement of details or a close verbal match.
State the claim narrowly. Distinguish a useful comparison from an identified source and from a proposed cipher input.

If the comparison suggests a key, use the reproduction guide to define the operation and scope. A bibliography entry does not establish that a technique has been tried; that belongs in documented experiment records.

Sources and coverage

This is a directory of the sourced comparisons currently developed in Liberpedia, not an exhaustive list of influences or a claim about the puzzle authors’ beliefs. Each linked article supplies its primary text, collection record, historical walkthrough, or named attribution. New candidates should be added with that evidence rather than grouped together solely because their themes seem compatible.


The transcendentalism background page explains Emerson’s intellectual setting and separates that context from the documented use of Self-Reliance in the book cipher.


For the terminology behind these comparisons, see Blake prints: plates, impressions, and copies. Its illustrated explanation separates the printing method from the identity of a particular source image.

title: Testing knowledge, certainty, and authority
summary: Read the warning alongside inward discovery, adherence, and the instruction to impose nothing on others.
text:
The warning asks readers to test what the book says. Later passages direct them inward, criticize adherence, and tell them to impose nothing on others. These are related instructions, but they do not all answer the same question: how to check a claim, how to understand oneself, and how to treat another person are different problems.

Read the instructions together

[Image: Original LP1-01 warning page]
The warning places testing beside a demand to preserve the book.
[Image: Original LP1-16 instruction page with a number panel below the text]
The final LP1 instruction combines inward discovery with a limit on imposing it on others.

	Passage	Instruction or claim	Question it raises

	Warning · LP1-01	Do not accept the book without testing knowledge and finding truth.	What would justify accepting a claim?

	Welcome · LP1-03–04	The journey promises an end to certainty; the reader is told to command their own self.	Can self-direction coexist with uncertainty?

	Loss of Divinity · LP1-10–13	Adherence can attach to dogma or reason when motivated by belonging and being right.	Why is a person accepting or defending an idea?

	Instruction · LP1-16	Question, discover truth within, follow it, and impose nothing on others.	Where does directing oneself end and directing others begin?


The table paraphrases whole sections. It does not assign every phrase to every page in a range. Follow the complete readings for literal text, contextual English, and decoding instructions.

Belief, truth, justification, and knowledge

Epistemology studies questions about knowledge and justified belief. These distinctions help unpack the warning’s demand to test, without assuming that the manuscript endorses a particular philosophical theory.

	Term	Question to ask	Research example

	Belief	What claim does the person accept?	“I think this mark is a separator.” That identifies a position, not its evidence.

	Truth	Is the claim actually the case?	For an integer sum greater than 1, being prime or composite does not depend on how strongly someone favors either answer.

	Justification	What grounds support accepting the claim?	A declared counting rule, preserved input and independently checked calculation support a numerical claim.

	Knowledge	What makes the acceptance more than a lucky or unsupported correct answer?	Guessing a prime sum correctly and demonstrating the calculation are different achievements.


The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy’s analysis of knowledge explains the familiar “justified true belief” account and objections to its sufficiency. It should not be presented as a settled definition. For the broader field, see its epistemology overview. These references explain vocabulary; they do not establish a source for Liber Primus.

The distinction becomes especially useful when a calculation is correct but its interpretation is uncertain. Verifying that a selected string has a prime sum supports that arithmetic result. It does not by itself establish why those boundaries were chosen, whether a spelling was selected after inspection, or whether the authors intended the sum. Those are additional claims requiring additional evidence. See prime-sum reproduction and selection and chance comparisons.

A worked example: what does a prime sum establish?

Consider CWESTIAN in the final LP1 instruction. Under the recorded Gematria Primus values, its seven runes give 13 + 19 + 67 + 53 + 59 + 107 + 29 = 347. The spelling and its arithmetic are documented in the word-sum comparison. What can we conclude from that result?

[Image: Three separate questions: verify the arithmetic, evaluate a pattern against a stated comparison, and investigate whether the authors deliberately arranged it.]
A research distinction applied to the manuscript, not a diagram supplied by it. Open full size · Download diagram (SVG).

The arithmetic claim is directly checkable. Add the seven values and test the resulting integer. Since the square root of 347 is less than 19, it is enough to check the prime divisors 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, and 17. None divides it, so 347 is prime. That conclusion concerns this exact sequence and counting rule.

The pattern claim needs a comparison. “This sum is prime” and “this is surprisingly rare” are different statements. A comparison might examine other words with a specified length and encoding, or a declared set of alternative spellings. Those choices produce different questions. If many words, boundaries, reversals, or spellings were inspected before choosing this example, the comparison must account for that search. See null models and selection effects; this example does not supply a probability estimate.

The intention claim needs evidence about a deliberate choice. The book’s attention to primes makes the question reasonable, but a prime total alone does not show that this spelling was chosen to produce it. An explicit instruction or a consistent rule that successfully predicts additional cases would provide further evidence to evaluate. A small chance estimate would still not, by itself, identify an author’s purpose.

A useful research note therefore preserves the verified total while leaving the stronger questions open. It states which claim has been checked, which comparison has been performed, and which interpretation is being proposed. This follows the warning’s invitation to examine claims without turning that invitation into a ready-made statistical method.

Questioning a book while preserving it

The warning both invites scrutiny and forbids changing the book’s words or numbers. Those demands need not be contradictory. A reader can reject an interpretation while keeping the source intact. In research, the practical counterpart is to preserve the original image and transcription, then record corrections and proposed transformations separately.

This is an application of the passage, not proof of its intended meaning. It also explains why “the book tells us to do this” is not sufficient evidence for a solution: the warning itself withholds unconditional authority from the book. A proposed decoding still needs a defined input, a repeatable operation, and a way to distinguish its output from an attractive coincidence. See documenting a reproducible attempt.

Certainty is not the same as correctness

The Welcome includes certainty among the things the journey brings to an end. Read with the warning, this makes confidence an unreliable substitute for checking. That does not mean the text proves that knowledge is impossible. It can instead be read as challenging the reader’s attachment to already having the answer.

The first koan gives this tension a narrative form: the student offers increasingly abstract descriptions of himself, but admission follows his inability to finish an answer. The story supplies no final definition for a solver to insert. Its unresolved ending is part of the passage, not a blank that the wiki should silently fill.

Why “dogma or reason” matters

The Loss of Divinity criticizes following either dogma or reason for the sake of belonging and being right. Omitting “reason” would turn this into a simpler criticism of religious authority than the recorded text supports. The stated problem concerns the motive for adherence, not only the kind of argument followed.

In a research setting, agreement with a respected solver and a compelling calculation can both deserve examination. The calculation should remain independently checkable. Conversely, disagreeing with a group is not evidence that an alternative is correct. The manuscript’s language can motivate scrutiny without serving as a verdict on any particular hypothesis. For the surrounding account of dependence and identity, see circumference.

Inward truth and other people

LP1-16 places inward discovery and following one’s truth beside the instruction to impose nothing on others. One interpretation is that personal conviction does not automatically authorize control of another person. The Welcome’s instruction to command one’s own self supports that comparison.

“Truth inside yourself” does not settle how two incompatible factual claims should be evaluated. The passage offers no formal theory of truth. It would be too strong to label it a proof of relativism, or to conclude that a preferred cipher result needs no external check. Personal interpretation and a public claim about what a sequence decodes to have different evidential requirements.

Three instructions about directing oneself
The comparison becomes clearer when each instruction stays attached to its page. The excerpts below join words split by manuscript line breaks but retain the literal reading’s spelling. They are not substituted English spellings for prime-sum calculations.
LP1-04: COMMAND-YOUR-OWN-SELF. This short red line follows the passage about being a law unto oneself and the holiness of each intelligence. Its object is the reader’s own self. The text does not provide a practical program of habits or exercises here.
LP1-13: PROGRAM-YOUR-MIND.PROGRAM-REALITY. This follows the advice about wealth and attachment. The first command concerns the mind; the second extends the claim to reality. That extension needs interpretation: the phrase alone cannot establish a physical mechanism by which thought changes external events. See the close reading of this instruction.
LP1-16: FOLLOW-YOUR-TRUTH.IMPOSE-NOTHNG-ON-OTHERS. The final command supplies a boundary alongside personal conviction. Read together, the two sentences can support self-direction without treating another person’s agreement as something the reader is entitled to demand.
[Image: The small red instruction on LP1-04, read as AN INSTRUCTIAN. COMMAND YOUR OWN SELF.]
The first instruction is easy to miss below the main text. Inspect its location and original image.
What this comparison supports: the known readings repeatedly address how a reader directs their own thinking and conduct, and explicitly place a limit on imposition. What remains interpretive: whether those passages form one consistent ethical system, what “reality” means in LP1-13, and how the authors would resolve a conflict between inward conviction and public evidence. The book does not spell out those answers in these instructions.
For research, keep that distinction practical. A personal reading can explain why a passage matters to someone; a claim that a particular cipher produces that passage must still identify its input, operation and output. Neither individual certainty nor agreement from a group supplies the missing calculation.
Locate the wording yourself

The concordance searches the preserved contextual readings. Even that layer retains some unconventional spellings: the final instruction uses KWESTION. An exact search for question returns no hits in this snapshot; that is a spelling limitation, not evidence that the idea is absent.

python scripts/reading_concordance.py "believe"
python scripts/reading_concordance.py "kwestion"
python scripts/reading_concordance.py "impose"

Expected counts are 3, 1, and 1. KWESTION begins at contextual word 3 of the instruction; IMPOSE begins at word 13. These are one-based word positions, not rune offsets. For numerical work, return to the literal rune sequence and the spelling and prime-sum evidence.

For a closer reading of the three behaviors and the advice about wealth, see consumption, preservation, and adherence.

Sources and limits

This guide is an internal comparison of the nine recorded contextual sections, with literal readings and images linked above. The interpretations are editorial analysis, not additional plaintext. Emerson’s Self-Reliance provides a separately documented earlier-puzzle reference and a useful comparison; shared concerns about conformity do not establish that Emerson is the source of these instructions. Continue with the wider philosophical themes.

title: William Blake and The Marriage of Heaven and Hell
summary: The holy-life sentence on LP1-04, its literary parallel, and the limits of source and artwork attribution.
text:
LP1-04 contains a close verbal parallel to the ending of William Blake's The Marriage of Heaven and Hell. It is a concrete comparison worth following; it does not establish that every philosophical or visual feature of Liber Primus comes from Blake.

The wording, side by side

	Source	Text	Location

	Liber Primus, contextual English	FOR ALL THAT LIVES IS HOLY	LP1-04, after the statement about each intelligence

	Blake	For everything that lives is holy.	Final sentence of the Chorus following A Song of Liberty


The wording is close but not identical: “all” replaces “everything.” The literal manuscript labels read FOR-ALL-THAT-LIUES-IS-HOLY after joining the archive's line wrap. LIVES is the contextual interpretation of LIUES, not an extra change to the rune stream. See the complete Welcome reading and literal-reading conventions.

Check the external sentence in Project Gutenberg's transcription of the 1906 edition, under Chorus near the end. This edition's printed page numbers are not identifiers for the original illuminated plates.

What the comparison supports

The shared wording supports describing this as a close verbal parallel and a plausible Blake allusion. The manuscript passage does not name Blake. A parallel cannot establish whether the authors consulted his work directly, encountered a quotation elsewhere, or intended the surrounding book to function as a key. Those are separate hypotheses.

For cipher work, a possible reference becomes a candidate source only after specifying a rule. Which edition, passage, characters, normalization and transformation? Choosing these after seeing promising fragments changes the scope of the test. Use the reproducibility guide and Have we tried it? to distinguish a source comparison from a documented technique test.

Read the surrounding argument

Blake's work also treats inward divinity and the limits of perception. In The Voice of the Devil, reason is described in relation to the outward circumference of energy. These provide additional comparison points with Liber Primus's Loss of Divinity and second koan. They are thematic or vocabulary comparisons, weaker than the closely matched final sentence. Similar words do not ensure identical meanings.

Within Liber Primus, the holy-life statement follows claims about the individual and intelligence, and precedes an instruction to command oneself. In Blake, the sentence closes a Chorus addressing religious authority and restrictions. Reading both settings prevents the shared line from becoming an isolated code token with no literary context. The philosophical themes guide traces the manuscript's internal connections.

Why the title joins Heaven and Hell

Before The Voice of the Devil, the 1906 edition, printed page 7, presents opposing forces as necessary to human existence. Its examples pair attraction with repulsion, reason with energy, and love with hate. It then associates religious labels of good and evil with passive obedience to reason and active energy. This prepares the reader for the reversal of familiar moral expectations in the next section.

Contraries here are opposing forces in the argument, not simply a logical error to be corrected. The text gives both sides a role in progression. Reading only the later circumference sentence can obscure that setting: reason appears within a relationship to energy, not as an isolated dictionary definition of a bad thing.

For Liber Primus, this suggests a question rather than an answer: does its criticism of adherence to reason concern the faculty itself, or the wish to belong and be right? Its wording specifies the latter motive. Do not substitute Blake’s opposition for the manuscript’s argument merely because both mention reason. Compare the complete passages before proposing a shared philosophical system.

The shared word “circumference”

In The Voice of the Devil, Blake describes reason as the “bound or outward circumference of Energy.” The sentence is on printed page 8 of the linked 1906 transcription. Its immediate subject is the relationship between body, soul, energy, and reason; “circumference” supplies a boundary metaphor.

Compare that with the manuscript’s three circumference passages. The Loss of Divinity assigns behaviors to the circumference. The second koan associates it with the voice of the I. The parable asks for circumferences to be shed. These are different grammatical and narrative uses, even though they share the unusual term and a possible idea of limitation.

	Comparison	What the wording supports	What remains unestablished

	Blake’s outward circumference and the manuscript’s circumference	A specific vocabulary parallel worth examining beside the known holy-life parallel.	That the manuscript uses “circumference” as an exact synonym for Blake’s reason.

	Reason in the two works	Both texts place reason in a critical discussion rather than treating it as an unquestioned authority.	That their criticism has the same target: the manuscript explicitly questions following reason for belonging and being right.
