LP2-17–21 each contain twelve rows of black runes within broad blank margins. The crossed-loop drawing on LP2-15 is not repeated on these sheets. Their page records now include regions you can open in the image inspector: 17, 18, 19, 20, and 21.
A spacing difference on LP2-21
On LP2-21, a wider gap separates the second and third rows. That is a layout observation, not a decoded paragraph break. If you test a rule that resets at this gap, record the reset as an assumption and compare its result with the same rule without the reset.
[Image: First three rows of LP2-21, showing the wider gap after row two.]
Upper text block of LP2-21. Compare the spacing between the first two rows with the gap before the third. Read the full sheet · Original JPEG.
Punctuation is a separate layer
Small dots and compact dotted clusters occur among the runes and sometimes at the start of a row. Examples include the start of row three on LP2-19 and row seven on LP2-20. The dots guide explains why visual marks and transcription punctuation need to be distinguished. For rune-only statistics such as index of coincidence, punctuation is excluded from the symbol counts. A study of spacing or separators needs to preserve that information separately; excluding it from one calculation does not show that it has no role.
The closing page: crossbars and a reclining figure
LP2-22 looks quite different from the opening number panel. Six rows of black runes end in a small red dotted mark. Under the text sits a dark horizontal drawing with three thick crossbars; farther down, a reclining human figure extends across the bottom edge, feet to the left and head to the right.
[Image: Lower portion of LP2-22: the dark three-crossbar drawing above a reclining human figure.]
Detail of the original LP2-22 image, from below the text to the bottom edge. Read the full page · Download the original JPEG
The figure is a useful feature to search for and compare, but an identification needs more than a resemblance. Its posture alone cannot establish a death scene, a named person, or a borrowed composition. The page record has separate inspection regions for the red mark, the crossbar drawing, and the figure.
Reclining figures also appear along the bottoms of LP1-14–16. On LP1-14, the figure sits beneath the second koan on LP1-14. On all three LP1 sheets the head is on the left and the feet on the right, opposite to LP2-22. This gives a concrete comparison across the two releases, without establishing that the images are exact reflections or that their accompanying texts share a cipher.
[Image: Bottom of LP1-14: reclining human figure with head on the left and feet on the right.]
Bottom 600 pixels of the original LP1-14 sheet. Read the full page · Original JPEG.
Even within this grouping, layouts vary. LP2-16, immediately after the panel page, has twelve rows of black text and no separate illustration. Treat the community section name as a way to locate these sheets; whether their text shares a key or transformation remains a separate question.
Following the numerical details
The panel contains sixteen numbers; 3299 is red. The panel article gives every value, row and column totals, and a reproducible calculation. For an idea involving prime positions or reversed digits, use prime indices and emirps before assigning those operations to the drawing.
There is also a literal MOBIUS in the known Some Wisdom reading. That textual occurrence is a separate piece of evidence. A shared name is a reason to compare the pages, not proof that one supplies a key for the other.
Sources and further reading
Cicada Solvers’ LP2 index supplies the community section names and ranges. The page links above provide original images, checksums, and pinned archive sources. Section names are descriptive navigation labels, not decrypted headings.
Return to the illustrated index to compare other manuscript motifs.

The reclining-figure comparison brings the four manuscript locations together and explains the published proposal involving Jung's Red Book, including the source checks still needed.

title: Cuneiform-like mark
summary: Compare the repeated mark on LP2-33–39, including its different placement on the first page.
text:
A compact, two-row mark repeats on LP2-33–39. It is commonly called the cuneiform mark. The visible mark belongs in an illustrated index even though its intended meaning is not established.
[Image: Two-row cuneiform-like mark from LP2-33, displayed in its original orientation]
LP2-33 · Below the runic text. Cropped view of the original; no rotation or reflection. Complete sheet · Original JPEG
[Image: Two-row cuneiform-like mark from LP2-34, displayed in its original orientation]
LP2-34 · Above the runic text. Cropped view of the original; no rotation or reflection. Complete sheet · Original JPEG
Where to find it
Placement matters. On LP2-33 the mark is at the bottom; on LP2-34–39 it is above the main text. Calling it a “header” without that exception would hide a potentially relevant layout difference. The previews below let you compare all seven sheets.
[Image: LP2-33 manuscript preview]
LP2-33 · Read
[Image: LP2-34 manuscript preview]
LP2-34 · Read
[Image: LP2-35 manuscript preview]
LP2-35 · Read
[Image: LP2-36 manuscript preview]
LP2-36 · Read
[Image: LP2-37 manuscript preview]
LP2-37 · Read
[Image: LP2-38 manuscript preview]
LP2-38 · Read
[Image: LP2-39 manuscript preview]
LP2-39 · Read
What the name tells us
The British Museum’s Mesopotamia guide explains how early pictograms developed into wedge-shaped writing called cuneiform. Here it is the community’s name for a visual resemblance. Identifying the manuscript mark as a particular historical sign would require a sign-by-sign comparison with a specified script, period, orientation, and reading. The label alone is not a translation.
The repeated motif is also not part of the ordinary 29-rune Gematria Primus alphabet. Do not assign it a rune index or prime value merely because it occurs beside runic text.
Is cuneiform a language?

Cuneiform is a writing system, not the name of one language. Sumerian, Akkadian, and Hittite were among the languages written with it. Oxford’s Electronic Text Corpus of Sumerian Literature explains that signs could represent words (logograms) or sounds, including syllables (phonograms). A sign could have several reading values; surrounding language and context help determine which one applies.

That distinction matters when investigating this manuscript. Even a convincing match to a historical sign would leave questions about its reading and use here. “It resembles cuneiform” does not tell us whether the mark represents a word, a sound, a decorative motif, or an instruction.

From resemblance to a proposed reading

The following steps separate claims that are easy to blur together. They are a way to document a comparison, not a decipherment of the mark.

	Claim	What to show

	Visual resemblance	Place the manuscript detail beside the proposed comparison. Preserve orientation and show every rotation or reflection you introduce.

	Historical sign identification	Cite a sign list or documented inscription, its date and writing tradition. Explain both matching features and differences.

	Chosen reading	State the language and reading value you select. Explain why you choose it over alternatives.

	Use in Liber Primus	Show how the proposed reading relates to the surrounding page. A historical meaning alone does not establish the puzzle’s intended use.


Transliteration records a reading in another writing system; translation expresses meaning in another language. Neither is simply tracing the wedges. In Liberpedia’s transcription guide, the immediate task is more limited: record what is visibly present before interpreting it. Keep a proposed reading separate from that record, and describe any test using the experiment documentation guide.

Reading a sign list’s notation

A number in a scholarly label need not be a number written in the ancient text. Oxford’s ETCSL introduction explains these conventions:

	Notation or term	What it distinguishes

	gu, gu₂, gu₃	Different signs sharing a phonetic value: homophony. The subscripts distinguish readings; they are not quantities.

	Determinative	A category marker, such as one preceding a deity’s name. Such markers are thought to have been unpronounced.

	Superscript	One way ETCSL displays a determinative in transliteration.


When recording a proposed comparison, preserve the source’s notation and explain it. Do not automatically treat its subscript as a cipher digit, an exponent or a Gematria Primus value. This glossary does not identify any of those signs in the Liber Primus motif.

Other details in this section
LP2-33 and LP2-39 show conspicuous separated black dots. LP2-36–38 include red decimal labels: 1 on page 36, 2–4 on page 37, and 5 on page 38. These observations help locate parts of the section; they do not establish what a dot or label instructs the reader to do. See dots and punctuation for the distinction between printed shapes and transcription notation.
Follow the red numbers across pages

	Page	Visible decimal labels	Placement

	LP2-36	1	At the start of a block below the opening text.

	LP2-37	2, 3, 4	At successive block starts, from top to bottom.

	LP2-38	5	Below the opening block, which has no new decimal label.


This sequence is useful for recording layout before testing a method. A page break, a new text block, and a printed number are separate observations. If you propose restarting a key at one of them, say which one and record its exact rune position. The visual sequence alone does not tell us whether any key should restart. See key advancement and counting conventions and red text and color boundaries.

How to compare repeated marks
The two detail views above use 420 × 440 pixel windows in their respective 2400 × 3600 originals. Coordinates below start at the upper-left corner, with x increasing rightward and y downward. Right and bottom bounds are excluded, as in the image-region convention.
	Page	Left, top	Right, bottom	Position on sheet
	LP2-33	1000, 3030	1420, 3470	Below the text
	LP2-34	1000, 130	1420, 570	Above the text
These are display windows, not measurements of the exact ink boundary. Equal window dimensions make the views easier to compare, but do not establish pixel equality. Open the complete sheets to examine their surrounding text and margins.
Download the original JPEGs from the page records.
Record a rectangle around each mark in original-image pixels. Include enough surrounding whitespace to preserve orientation.
Compare both appearance and placement. Scaling a preview for display is not evidence that the source marks have identical dimensions.
If testing pixel equality, state the alignment, scale, threshold, and compression tolerance. Visual similarity alone does not establish identical bytes.
The image-region guide explains coordinate and threshold conventions. This article records location and appearance; it does not claim a completed pixel-equality test or a decipherment.
Sources
Cicada Solvers’ LP2 index supplies the community section names and ranges. The page links above provide original images, checksums, and pinned archive sources. Section names are descriptive navigation labels, not decrypted headings.

For red headings, numbers, and marks, see rubrication and color boundaries, with illustrated examples and guidance for recording a proposed extraction.

title: Spirals and branching borders
summary: Compare the curled borders on LP2-03–07 with the branching designs on LP2-40–55, and plan a measurable geometric comparison.
text:
Several groups of Liber Primus pages have curled drawings beside the text. The community calls LP2-03–07 “Spirals,” LP2-40–53 “Spiral Branches,” and LP2-54–55 “Spiral & Dead Tree.” These names make the images easier to find. Comparing their actual linework is more useful than treating every curl as the same symbol.
The curled borders on LP2-03–07
On LP2-03, paired curves frame the left and right margins of the runic text. Each side has a tighter upper curl and a longer lower curve. LP2-07 retains this border arrangement, while its lower text ends above a red line and five large black dots.
[Image: LP2-03 cropped page preview]
LP2-03 · Read
[Image: LP2-07 cropped page preview]
LP2-07 · Read
The dots are a separate feature from the small groups of specks beside the upper curls. See dots and punctuation for examples of why position, size, and arrangement should be recorded separately.
Open the intervening pages: LP2-04 · LP2-05 · LP2-06.
The branching borders on LP2-40–55
LP2-40 has curls joined to branching, root-like forms on both sides of the text. LP2-53 shows a winged insect below its red closing passage. The next pair, LP2-54–55, continues the branching border style; LP2-55 also contains a pale tree-shaped drawing above a winged insect.
[Image: LP2-40 cropped page preview]
LP2-40 · Read
[Image: LP2-53 cropped page preview]
LP2-53 · Read
[Image: LP2-54 cropped page preview]
LP2-54 · Read
[Image: LP2-55 cropped page preview]
LP2-55 · Read
Use the illustrated index to inspect the intervening LP2-40–53 pages. The branches and trees article compares these forms with the narrow branching drawing on LP2-08–14.
Compare the group openings: LP2-40 and LP2-54

Both pages begin with an enlarged red rune beside three rows and smaller red text at the start of the first row. On LP2-54, the red opening ends with a compact punctuation cluster before the black runes continue. The shared border style does not erase these differences in text and punctuation.

Each page also has a small cluster beside the inner edge of each border. On the left, three marks are solid black and two are pale ring outlines; on the right, all five are solid. The same fill pattern is recorded on LP2-53, with enlarged views. This comparison covers these inspected pages, not every intervening page.

Open the LP2-40 observations or LP2-54 observations beside the original images. The pale tree and winged figure that explain the community name “Spiral & Dead Tree” are on LP2-55; the name does not mean both pages contain a tree.

A useful comparison starts with a question
	Question	What to record	What the result would establish
	Do two pages reuse the same border?	Original-file hashes, crop rectangles, alignment, and pixel differences	Agreement under the stated alignment and tolerance
	Are the two margins mirror images?	A defined reflection axis and corresponding points on both drawings	How closely the selected regions match after reflection
	Does a curl follow a particular spiral?	A centre, sampled points, coordinate scale, fitted parameters, and residuals	The quality of that geometric fit, compared with alternatives
For example, a logarithmic spiral has r = a exp(bθ), while an Archimedean spiral has r = a + bθ. Here r is distance from the chosen centre and θ is angle. Merely seeing a curl does not select either model. The chosen centre and the thickness of the drawn line can strongly affect a fit.
Before connecting geometry to a cipher, state how a measured result would change the decoding operation. “The borders look symmetric” and “read alternate lines backwards” are separate claims; the first does not supply the second without an explicit rule.
Preparing a reproducible image comparison
Choose the pages and the feature before fitting anything. Include a comparison page with a visibly different border.
Download the original files and verify their SHA-256 hashes.
Record rectangles using original-image coordinates. Keep the original pixels and any transformed comparison image separately.
Document scaling, rotation, reflection, thresholding, and the score used to compare the shapes.
Publish the script and output together, including mismatches. A visually plausible overlay alone is not enough to reproduce the comparison.
This article provides an inspection route and a comparison method. It does not report a completed geometric fit or establish a cipher role for the borders.
Sources
Page observations refer to the original JPEGs linked through the page records, which retain checksums and pinned archive sources. The section names and ranges follow Cicada Solvers’ LP2 index. Previews are cropped browsing aids; open a page record or reader for the complete image.

title: Branches and trees
summary: Locate the narrow branching drawings on LP2-08–14 and the pale tree on LP2-55; distinguish tips, junctions, and segments before counting.
text:
Branching forms occur in both releases. They differ in placement and appearance: a narrow drawing beside the text on LP2-08–14, curled borders later in the manuscript, and a pale tree-shaped drawing inside LP2-55. Keeping these examples separate makes it possible to compare them without losing their page context.
The leafy border on the Welcome pages
LP1-03 and LP1-04 place their text inside thick curving branches, with dense leaf shapes above and more open loops along the sides. Branches turn inward beneath the text. The broad arrangement is shared across the two sheets; describing that resemblance is not a pixel-level claim that every line is identical.
[Image: Top of LP1-03: thick branches and dense leaf-shaped forms meet above the text column.]
Top 650 pixels of LP1-03. Complete page · Original JPEG.
The Welcome reading spans both pages. Its language of pilgrimage and emergence gives textual context, but does not identify the plant forms or establish that the border encodes a route. Compare these enclosing branches with the separate margin drawing on LP2-08–14 below.
The small instruction at the bottom of LP1-04
Just above the lower border, LP1-04 has a line of red runes much smaller than the main writing. The known reading gives AN INSTRUCTIAN. COMMAND YOUR OWN SELF. This is visible text on the page, not an extracted hidden message.
[Image: LP1-04 detail: the small red runic instruction below the main passage.]
Original-image detail, rectangle [800, 2920, 800, 100]. Complete page · Original JPEG.
Use the complete reading and reproduction instructions to check how the line is decoded. Keeping it with the preceding text avoids losing a short instruction simply because it falls outside the main block. The comparison of self-direction instructions places this sentence beside LP1-13 and LP1-16. The red-writing guide explains why color and placement should be recorded separately from rune values.
The narrow branching drawing on LP2-08–14
LP2-08 shows a long, slender form along the left margin. Smaller lines branch off toward its upper and lower ends, while the main text sits to its right. LP2-14 shows the same broad arrangement and includes an insect drawing below the text at the right.
[Image: LP2-08 cropped page preview]
LP2-08 · Read
[Image: LP2-14 cropped page preview]
LP2-14 · Read
The community groups LP2-08–14 under “Branches.” Open the middle pages to compare placement and linework: 09 · 10 · 11 · 12 · 13. The group name does not establish that the form represents a particular plant species, diagram, or cipher key.
The branch changes sides on successive pages

Across this seven-page group, the branch alternates between the left and right margins. Read the sequence in archive order:

	Branch position	Pages

	Left of the text	08, 10, 12, 14

	Right of the text	09, 11, 13


[Image: LP2-08 with the branch to the left of the rune column]
LP2-08: left margin.
[Image: LP2-09 with the branch to the right of the rune column]
LP2-09: right margin.

A drawing can move to the other margin without being mirrored. To test reflection, compare corresponding tips, junctions, and bends after aligning the images; the left/right sequence alone does not answer that question. Likewise, a proposal to reverse text on alternating pages would be an additional operation to test, not something already demonstrated by this layout.

Curled borders and the pale tree
On LP2-40, branching forms are part of the curled drawings on both sides of the text. LP2-55 has that border style as well as a much lighter tree-shaped drawing in the central space above the insect. Its low contrast is itself a reason to consult the original image rather than relying on a transcription.
[Image: LP2-40 cropped page preview]
LP2-40 · Read
[Image: LP2-55 cropped page preview]
LP2-55 · Read
Compare the spiral and branching borders, or use the illustrated index to browse the other artwork groups, including the separately named LP2-27–32 “Wing & Tree” group.
The Wing and Tree group adds another distinct example: the soft-edged tree-shaped figure on LP2-32. It should not be conflated with the pale, more finely outlined drawing on LP2-55.
[Image: LP2-32: soft-edged tree-shaped drawing]
LP2-32 — soft-edged tree-shaped drawing. Open reader
Compare the two central tree drawings
These close views use equally wide regions of the original images. LP2-32 has broad, dark forms with soft edges. LP2-55 has much lighter, outlined contours with enclosed white spaces. The difference is already present in the preserved JPEGs; neither view has been sharpened or given extra contrast.
[Image: LP2-32: dark, soft-edged drawing in an unenhanced original-image detail.]
LP2-32: dark, soft-edged drawing. Full page.
[Image: LP2-55: pale, outlined drawing in an unenhanced original-image detail.]
LP2-55: pale, outlined drawing. Full page.
Both drawings have a trunk-like base and branching forms, but that resemblance does not yet establish reuse of one image. A proposed match needs corresponding bends, junctions, and proportions, with any transformations stated. Nor can this comparison tell us why one drawing is faint or the other soft-edged.
The page records offer an Inspect control for each tree. The selected rectangles are [650, 2050, 1100, 1150] on LP2-32 and [650, 1400, 1100, 1100] on LP2-55, in original-image pixels. They locate the drawings for inspection; they are not branch-count measurements.
What does “count the branches” mean?
A branch count sounds straightforward until two people trace the same drawing differently. One may count every visible line leaving a trunk; another may count terminal tips; a third may count each segment between junctions. Those are different measurements.
	Quantity	A possible explicit definition
	Tips	Endpoints of a traced line, excluding the boundary of the chosen crop
	Junctions	Locations where three or more traced segments meet
	Segments	Paths between tips or junctions, with no junction in their interior
	Main stem	A selected path identified by its endpoints and a stated selection rule
Under a graph representation, tips and junctions become vertices and the connecting segments become edges. A visually tree-like drawing need not yield a mathematical tree: a crossing may or may not be a connection, and a closed loop would change the graph. Publish an annotated tracing so another person can see those choices.
Handling the pale drawing on LP2-55
Increasing contrast can make a faint line easier to see, but it also changes the displayed pixels. Preserve the original file, label an enhanced image as a derivative, and record the operation. If a claim depends on a feature visible only after enhancement, show the corresponding unmodified region too.
For numerical work, choose the brightness threshold before counting and check how modest changes affect the result. A count that changes sharply with the threshold needs that sensitivity reported. The existing image-region guide explains thresholds used for other published measurements; those settings have not been validated as a segmentation method for this pale tree.
From appearance to interpretation
A botanical identification, a religious association, and a decoding instruction each require different evidence. A comparison with a named artwork should show the proposed source image and the matching features. A cipher proposal should specify how the drawing produces an ordered sequence or operation, rather than selecting a count because it happens to fit.
For wider interpretation, start with philosophical themes in the known readings. That article distinguishes what the text says from suggested connections. No particular symbolic meaning is assigned to these branching drawings here.
Paired plant borders on LP2-41–44
These four sheets each have twelve rows of black runes between tall curling stems. Look for the drooping narrow leaves, the root-like lower branches, and the groups of filled dots beside the stems. The page records provide original-image inspection regions: 41, 42, 43, and 44.
[Image: Plant borders flanking the runic text on LP2-41, with curled tips, drooping leaves, filled dots, and branching bases.]
Paired borders of LP2-41, original-image region [0, 760, 2400, 2100]. Complete sheet · Original JPEG.
A related border arrangement also frames the alphanumeric grids on LP2-49–51. This gives a visual comparison across different text layouts. It does not by itself establish identical artwork files, a plant species, or a shared cipher.
Keep the border dots separate from marks within the text. LP2-42 has paired short vertical strokes near the right ends of rows three and six; LP2-43 has a pair near the end of row one. Those observations are recorded on the individual pages. Their resemblance to familiar punctuation is not enough to assign a grammatical role; the punctuation guide explains how to preserve visual distinctions in an analysis.
The runic pages around the grids
The same broad border arrangement continues on LP2-45, 46, 47, and 48. Each has twelve runic rows. LP2-49–51 then place alphanumeric arrays inside the borders, before LP2-52 returns to a full twelve-row runic block.
	Pages	Central content
	LP2-45–48	Twelve runic rows on each sheet
	LP2-49–51	Alphanumeric grids; runic text above the first and below the last
	LP2-52	Twelve runic rows
That sequence is useful when defining a test's scope. A proposal based on the grid entries should say whether it also uses the surrounding runes or border marks. The change in central content does not by itself demonstrate a new key, cipher, or instruction to reset an operation.
There are also smaller differences worth inspecting. LP2-47 ends its first row with a dotted cluster. On LP2-48, small dots precede the first runes of rows four and six. The page records locate these examples in the originals; neither their placement nor the shared border assigns them a decoded meaning.
Sources
Page observations refer to the original JPEGs linked through the page records, which retain checksums and pinned archive sources. The section names and ranges follow Cicada Solvers’ LP2 index. Previews are cropped browsing aids; open a page record or reader for the complete image.

title: Insects and wing imagery
summary: Compare the opening-page insect, the LP2-14 profile, the Mayfly group, later winged figures, and the stippled drawing beneath the parable.
text:
Insect imagery appears in several different forms across both manuscript releases. A profile drawing, opposed figures, a detached wing, and the stippled figure beneath the final parable offer different visual evidence. This guide brings selected examples together so they can be compared without assuming that they depict the same animal.
Paired insects beside the warning
On LP1-01, two upright insect-like figures flank the middle of the warning text. Their heads are above their long striped wings, and they face inward. Curled stems and smaller ornaments occupy the outer margins. On LP1-15, another pair sits below the text instead; position is part of the comparison.
[Image: Middle of LP1-01: two upright insects face inward on opposite sides of the warning text.]
Original-image detail, rectangle [350, 1450, 1700, 750]. Complete page · Original JPEG.
The known warning reading and the embedded OutGuess content are different text layers associated with this image. Neither identifies the insects’ species. To test a proposed reuse of the LP1-15 figures, compare corresponding contours and internal markings after declaring any reflection or scaling.
The spread-wing insect on LP1-05
On LP1-05, a small insect-like figure sits between the Some Wisdom passage and the red heading above the mixed number grid. Its wings extend to both sides of a narrow central body. This makes it easy to distinguish from the sideways profiles on LP1-13 and LP1-16.
[Image: LP1-05 detail: a small insect-like figure with wings extending to either side of its central body.]
Original-image detail, rectangle [900, 1550, 600, 300]. Complete page · Original JPEG.
The known reading discusses primes and the totient function; the grid below the illustration converts rune words into a square with line sum 1033. Those are the figure’s visible textual surroundings. They do not identify its species or establish that a wing, body part, or orientation encodes a numerical operation.
When comparing this with the other insects, retain the page and crop coordinates. A spread-wing pose can obscure the profile features used elsewhere, so matching only the outline is weaker than matching detailed contours and internal markings.
The insect within the first koan’s frame
On LP1-09, a left-facing profile insect separates the end of the dialogue from the closing instruction. Its striped wing extends right. The whole page sits within the bearded-figure frame used on LP1-06–09.
[Image: LP1-09 detail: a horizontal profile insect with its head to the left and striped wing to the right.]
Original-image detail, rectangle [820, 1900, 750, 350]. Complete sheet · Original JPEG.
The complete first-koan reading supplies the surrounding dialogue and instruction. Compare this orientation with LP1-13, whose insect faces right, and LP1-16, whose insect faces left. Orientation describes what is visible; an exact rotation, reflection or shared source requires a separate image comparison.
The insect between passages on LP1-13
The small insect on LP1-13 faces right, with a dark head and a striped wing extending left over its body. It sits below the last two rows of the preceding argument and above the red opening of the Some Wisdom passage. The hooded figures around the page form a separate surrounding decoration.
[Image: LP1-13 detail: a black profile insect facing right with a striped wing extending left.]
Original-image detail from rectangle [820, 1050, 750, 300]. Full page · Original JPEG.
Its orientation and wing markings invite comparison with LP2-02 below. Those similarities do not establish a shared source image or biological species. Keep the two page records separate when recording a proposed match.
The pair on LP1-15 and the profile on LP1-16

The final pages of LP1 change the arrangement. LP1-15, which closes the second koan, places two upright insect-like figures below the text. Their heads are at the top, their striped wings extend downward, and they face inward toward one another. On LP1-16, a single horizontal insect faces left between the opening instruction and the number panel.

[Image: LP1-15: paired upright insects beneath the closing text of the second koan.]
LP1-15: paired figures, heads above wings.
[Image: LP1-16: a left-facing insect between the instruction and a five-by-five number panel.]
LP1-16: a horizontal figure, head left.

Both sheets also have a reclining human figure along the bottom edge. The reclining-figure comparison connects this motif with LP1-14 and LP2-22.
Compare these with the right-facing insect on LP1-13 above. Orientation is a useful first observation, but a shared striped wing is not enough to prove that one drawing was rotated or reflected to produce another. A reproducible comparison would preserve the originals, identify matching contours and internal marks, and state every transformation.
The complete instruction reading supplies the text beside the LP1-16 image and its number panel. The worked square calculation checks its 3301 line sums and half-turn symmetry. Readable text gives context for an illustration; it does not by itself establish the illustration’s intended meaning.

The insect below LP2-02

The opening group ends with a winged insect-like figure beneath the text on LP2-02. Its head faces right. A rounded eye and projecting appendages appear at that end; a large wing with dark internal stripes extends left. The page’s cross-like margin drawings remain separate from the figure.

[Image: Detail from LP2-02: a striped wing extends left from an insect-like body whose head faces right.]
Detail of the original LP2-02 JPEG, displayed from pixel rectangle [850, 2600, 750, 380]. No sharpening or thresholding is applied. See the complete page · Download original JPEG.

Compare its orientation and wing markings with the LP2-14 profile below. These descriptions make the two drawings easier to locate; they do not identify either as the source of the other or establish a species. The opening-page artwork comparison places the figure beside the loops and margin drawings on LP2-00–02.

The profile drawing on LP2-14
Below the text at the right of LP2-14 is a sideways insect drawing. The body is segmented, a veined wing rises above it, and long curved appendages extend from its rear. The narrow branching drawing continues down the opposite margin. This combination makes the page recognizable even without reading its runes.
[Image: LP2-14: profile insect beside the branching margin]
LP2-14 — profile insect beside the branching margin. Open reader
The “Mayfly” group: LP2-23–26
The community groups LP2-23–26 under “Mayfly.” LP2-23 opens with five large dots above the text. On LP2-24–26, elongated insect-like figures flank the text on both sides. Their upper and lower parts oppose one another, which makes orientation a useful feature to record before comparing the drawings.
[Image: LP2-23: five dots above the opening text]
LP2-23 — five dots above the opening text. Open reader
[Image: LP2-24: opposed figures beside the text]
LP2-24 — opposed figures beside the text. Open reader
[Image: LP2-25: the figures beside another text layout]
LP2-25 — the figures beside another text layout. Open reader
[Image: LP2-26: the final page of the community group]
LP2-26 — the final page of the community group. Open reader
The browsing name does not prove a species identification. Nor does it mean that a complete insect drawing appears on every page in the named group. The dot inventory separately records the LP2-23 arrangement.
Winged figures on later pages
LP2-53 and LP2-55 show dark winged figures beneath their text, within the surrounding curled borders. LP2-55 also has a pale tree-shaped drawing above its insect. On LP2-57, the figure is built from a dense vertical body and scattered marks extending into wing-like areas. Its rendering differs visibly from the outlined and shaded figures on pages 53 and 55.
[Image: LP2-53: winged figure beneath the red passage]
LP2-53 — winged figure beneath the red passage. Open reader
[Image: LP2-55: pale tree above a winged figure]
LP2-55 — pale tree above a winged figure. Open reader
[Image: LP2-57: stippled figure beneath the parable]
LP2-57 — stippled figure beneath the parable. Open reader
A resemblance between two figures is a starting point for comparison. To claim that they reuse one source, compare corresponding contours, internal details, and proportions after stating any scaling or reflection. Repeated subject matter alone is insufficient.
The detached wing
LP2-27 places a long, veined wing above the red opening text. It is useful to inspect that wing separately from the whole-insect drawings. The Wing and Tree guide follows the LP2-27–32 group from this image to the tree-shaped drawing on its last page.
Connecting the images with the text
The known Welcome and final parable use the word instar. An instar is a stage between molts, not the name of a species. The parable’s language of tunneling, shedding, and emergence makes an insect comparison relevant, but it does not identify every drawing in the book as a cicada.
This distinction leaves room for close reading. Ask which visual features accompany a readable passage, then ask how the passage uses its biological analogy. On unsolved pages, there is no established reading to supply that same context.
Mayfly and cicada: compare features, not just names

The community name “Mayfly” and the puzzle’s name “Cicada” should not be used interchangeably as identifications. The University of Kentucky’s mayfly guide and Purdue Entomology’s cicada account provide useful biological comparisons:

	Feature	Mayflies	Cicadas

	Immature habitat	Aquatic young, often called naiads.	Nymphs develop underground.

	Visible adult features	Two or three long tail filaments; forewings much larger than the hindwings, which may be absent.	A relatively stout body and largely transparent wings extending beyond it.

	Transition to the adult	A winged intermediate stage, the subimago, molts again before sexual maturity.	The emerging nymph climbs a support and sheds its nymphal covering.


Subimago names that intermediate winged mayfly stage. It is not another word for the discarded shell or for every insect’s immature stage. Compare instar, ecdysis and exuvia before applying one of these terms to a drawing.

For a manuscript comparison, record which features you can actually see. Long rear appendages may make a mayfly comparison worth investigating, but an artist’s line is not automatically an anatomical structure. A hidden or omitted hindwing cannot be counted as proof that the animal lacked it. Body proportions can also be changed by perspective or stylization. The habitat of an animal cannot be read from an isolated outline unless the image supplies environmental evidence.

This comparison explains what to look for; it does not identify a species, a source illustration, or the intended meaning of the manuscript. Likewise, the word instar in a readable passage does not tell us which insect is pictured beside it. The two university references were checked on 20 October 2026; their biological descriptions are background, not evidence of a historical connection to the puzzle authors.

What a defensible identification needs
	Evidence to retain	Why it matters
	The original page and an unmodified region	Shows which features are actually present, including faint lines and cropping
	A named comparison source	Lets another reader inspect the proposed illustration or anatomical reference
	Matching and nonmatching details	Prevents a general silhouette from outweighing contradictory features
	Orientation and transformations	Explains any rotation, reflection, stretching, or contrast changes used in the comparison
For an artwork-source attribution, a matching historical illustration is stronger evidence than a broad biological resemblance. For a species claim, diagnostic anatomy matters more than the puzzle’s name. Neither kind of identification automatically determines a cipher operation.
Sources and scope
Observations refer to the preserved JPEGs linked through the page records. Those records provide original files, SHA-256 hashes, and pinned public archive sources. Group names follow the Cicada Solvers LP2 index; they are community browsing labels, not decrypted chapter headings. Previews are cropped: open the reader to inspect complete pages.
This is a selected visual inventory, not an exhaustive survey of every insect depiction in Cicada 3301’s puzzles.

title: Wing and Tree: LP2-27–32
summary: Follow the detached wing and tree-shaped drawing at the endpoints of the LP2-27–32 group, with all intervening pages.
text:
“Wing & Tree” is the community name for LP2-27–32. The group begins with a detached, veined wing above the text on LP2-27 and ends with a soft-edged tree-shaped drawing below the text on LP2-32. Looking at the two endpoints makes the browsing name much easier to understand.
The illustrated endpoints
[Image: LP2-27: a detached wing above the runes]
LP2-27 — a detached wing above the runes. Open reader
[Image: LP2-32: a tree-shaped drawing below the runes]
LP2-32 — a tree-shaped drawing below the runes. Open reader
The wing has a dark outer boundary and a network of internal lines. The tree-shaped drawing has a dark central trunk-like form and branching extensions, with much softer edges. These descriptions concern appearance; they do not establish a species, a source illustration, or an intended mathematical structure.
The pages between them
LP2-28–31 carry the intervening runic text. Keep these pages in view when proposing a section-wide operation: a rule that uses only the illustrated endpoints still needs to explain how it applies to the middle.
[Image: LP2-28: intervening text]
LP2-28 — intervening text. Open reader
[Image: LP2-29: intervening text]
LP2-29 — intervening text. Open reader
[Image: LP2-30: intervening text]
LP2-30 — intervening text. Open reader
[Image: LP2-31: intervening text]
LP2-31 — intervening text. Open reader
Reading the middle pages as images
Each of LP2-28, LP2-29, LP2-30 and LP2-31 has twelve rows of black runes in a central block with broad blank margins. None of these four sheets has the detached wing or tree drawing found at the endpoints, an illustrated border, or a visible red heading. Small single dots and compact punctuation clusters remain part of their visual layout.
For specific details, inspect the dot at the start of LP2-28’s fourth row, clusters in LP2-29’s third and fourth rows, the opening dot on LP2-30’s final row, and clusters in LP2-31’s first two rows. Each observation links to a rectangle in the original image.
Row boundaries, punctuation and rune counts answer different questions. The index-of-coincidence example uses LP2-31’s 269 runes, excluding punctuation. The repeated-sequence guide likewise explains its rune-only stream. Those exclusions define the calculations; they do not establish that the excluded marks are meaningless. For a layout-based test, preserve their positions and state whether a sequence continues across a row or page break.
Two different kinds of branching
The wing’s internal lines form enclosed areas; the tree-shaped drawing suggests a central form with extensions. A graph can represent either tracing, but the decision about vertices and edges must be explicit. A junction, a crossing, and a closed cell are different features.
The branches and trees article defines tips, junctions, and segments as separate possible measurements. For the wing, a cell count would be another measurement: state whether the outer boundary closes a region and how faint or interrupted lines are handled. Counting a picture without those rules is difficult to reproduce.
Inspecting the soft-edged drawing
Use the original LP2-32 JPEG to inspect the tree-shaped figure. Enlarging it changes display size; it does not recover additional detail. Sharpening or thresholding can change apparent branch boundaries, so any transformed image should be shown alongside the original and identified as a derivative.
If testing a proposed source image, retain the source’s provenance and show the alignment. If measuring the manuscript alone, record the crop rectangle and test whether modest threshold changes alter the count. The image-region guide explains how to preserve those decisions.
Connecting a visual proposal to a cipher test
A test needs more than a plausible resemblance between wing veins and branches. Specify the ordered values or operation extracted from the drawing, the pages it applies to, and any reset or reading-direction rule. Record those choices before examining candidate plaintext. See documenting a reproducible attempt.
This article does not report a successful decoding or a completed geometric test. The experiment registry is the place to check documented tests once reviewed records are available.

Sources
